nodes.label: Keys
nodes.body: This branch of the chapter starts from a payment. Alice wants to pay Bob, but the thousands of full nodes that will verify her transaction do not know who Alice or Bob are, and the design is meant to keep it that way, to protect their privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice therefore has to tell the network that Bob should receive some of her bitcoins without tying any part of the transaction to Bob's real-world identity, and without linking it to the other payments Bob receives. The method must also guarantee that only Bob can spend what he receives afterwards. Keys are the answer to both demands, and the rest of the chapter is the story of how a key becomes something that one person can hand to another.

paras.text: This branch of the chapter starts from a payment. Alice wants to pay Bob, but the thousands of full nodes that will verify her transaction do not know who Alice or Bob are, and the design is meant to keep it that way, to protect their privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice therefore has to tell the network that Bob should receive some of her bitcoins without tying any part of the transaction to Bob's real-world identity, and without linking it to the other payments Bob receives. The method must also guarantee that only Bob can spend what he receives afterwards. Keys are the answer to both demands, and the rest of the chapter is the story of how a key becomes something that one person can hand to another.

Without keys there would be no way to decide who may spend a coin. A bank answers that question by looking up an account holder in its own records, but a network of nodes that do not trust one another has no such record and no such authority. Bitcoin replaces the account holder with a pair of numbers: whoever can produce a valid signature with the right private number may spend, and anyone can check the signature with the matching public number. The original Bitcoin paper describes this in its simplest form, in which a receiver like Bob accepts bitcoins to a public key in a transaction that the spender signs, and in which full nodes verify that the spender's signature commits to the output of a hash function that itself commits to Bob's public key and the other transaction details (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

You meet keys every time you use a wallet. Chapter 1 described the wallet as the software through which people use Bitcoin and explained that in a noncustodial wallet only the user holds the keys. Chapter 2 showed that a transaction input carries a digital signature and an output receives funds. This chapter opens those two ideas up: it shows what the signature is made from, how the number that stands behind a payment is generated, and why the strings that people actually copy, such as an address, look the way they do.

The branch is arranged as the book arranges its argument. The key pair section introduces public key cryptography, the digital signature, the private key and the public key. The randomness section explains where a private key must come from. The curve section describes the mathematics that turns a private key into a public key, and the hash function section describes the second tool, which lets a long public key be replaced by a short commitment. Later branches of the chapter combine these ingredients into the addresses that modern Bitcoin software uses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two warnings run through everything that follows. The private key must stay secret at all times, because revealing it to a third party is equivalent to giving that party control over the bitcoins it secures. It must also be backed up and protected from accidental loss, because a lost private key cannot be recovered and the funds it secured are lost for good (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Secrecy and survival are the whole of key management.

nodes.label: Key pair
nodes.body: A key pair is the combination of a private key and a public key that belongs to it. In Bitcoin the key pair is what controls access to bitcoins: the public key is used to receive funds, and the private key is used to sign transactions that spend them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The two keys are not independent. The public key is calculated from the private key, and the mathematical relationship between them is what allows the private key to produce signatures that anyone can validate against the public key without learning the private key.

paras.text: A key pair is the combination of a private key and a public key that belongs to it. In Bitcoin the key pair is what controls access to bitcoins: the public key is used to receive funds, and the private key is used to sign transactions that spend them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The two keys are not independent. The public key is calculated from the private key, and the mathematical relationship between them is what allows the private key to produce signatures that anyone can validate against the public key without learning the private key.

The pair is the smallest unit of ownership that Bitcoin knows. A wallet, in the words of the book, contains a collection of key pairs, each consisting of a private key and a public key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Every question about who may spend a given output reduces to the question of who holds the private key of the pair that the output was paid to, which is why this second level of the branch deserves careful reading.

The pair works in one direction only, and everything else follows from that. The private key is simply a very large whole number, chosen at random; the public key is obtained by adding a fixed point on the curve to itself that many times, an operation the next level of the chapter sets out in full. Computing forward is cheap, because doubling and adding reach any multiple in a few hundred steps rather than in as many steps as the number is large. Computing backward - recovering the multiplier from the result - has no comparable shortcut, and that asymmetry is the whole of the protection. It also explains the book's tip that a wallet need store only the private key: the public key is not a second secret to be guarded but a value that can be recalculated from the first whenever it is wanted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets the pair wherever a wallet is created or a key is moved. A new wallet reports the keys it has made rather than their values; an export writes the private key out in a text form and leaves the public key to be recomputed; a block explorer shows the public side, or a commitment to it, because that is the half which has to travel. The pair is met again in every later chapter of this course: the signature of chapter 2 is made with the private half and checked with the public half, and the tree of keys in chapter 5 is a way of making very many pairs from one secret (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two cautions. The names mislead a little: a public key is public only once it has been used, and a wallet that hands out a fresh commitment for each payment is deliberately keeping it back, for reasons the section on address reuse gives. And the pair is not an identity. It proves that whoever signs holds the private key; it says nothing about who that is, nor about whether the key is still in the hands it was in yesterday. Treating a key as a person is the mistake behind most of the losses this chapter's later sections warn about (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Public key cryptography
nodes.body: Public key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, is a branch of cryptography in which every participant has two different but mathematically related keys. The book dates its invention to the 1970s and calls it a mathematical foundation for modern computer and information security (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Several suitable mathematical functions have been found since, among them the exponentiation of prime numbers and the multiplication of points on an elliptic curve. What they share is that they are easy to calculate in one direction and infeasible to calculate in the opposite direction with the computers and algorithms available today, and Bitcoin uses elliptic curve addition and multiplication as the basis of its cryptography (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Public key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, is a branch of cryptography in which every participant has two different but mathematically related keys. The book dates its invention to the 1970s and calls it a mathematical foundation for modern computer and information security (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Several suitable mathematical functions have been found since, among them the exponentiation of prime numbers and the multiplication of points on an elliptic curve. What they share is that they are easy to calculate in one direction and infeasible to calculate in the opposite direction with the computers and algorithms available today, and Bitcoin uses elliptic curve addition and multiplication as the basis of its cryptography (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reason Bitcoin needs the technique is easy to misjudge. It is not used to encrypt, that is to make secret, the transactions: everything on the blockchain is public. Its useful property is the ability to generate digital signatures. A private key applied to a transaction produces a numerical signature that only someone who knows the private key can produce, yet anyone who has the public key and the transaction can verify it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That is precisely what a network of strangers needs, because it makes it possible for everyone to verify every signature on every transaction while only the owners of private keys can create valid ones.

The technique is met wherever people need to prove something to others who do not trust them, and Chapter 3 has already shown one case: the signatures on the release files that a Bitcoin Core user checks before running the software. In Bitcoin itself the technique appears in two places. The spender's signature in a transaction input is checked against a public key, and the public key itself is hidden behind an address until the moment it is spent, as later sections of this chapter explain.

The mechanism has three steps. A private key, which is only a number, is chosen at random. A one-way function, elliptic curve multiplication in Bitcoin, turns it into the public key. When a transaction must be authorised, the private key is used to compute a signature over the transaction, and a verifier combines the signature, the transaction and the public key to decide whether the signature is genuine. The private key itself never leaves the signer's hands and is not revealed by the signature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin has traditionally used the ECDSA signature scheme over the secp256k1 curve with SHA256 hashes, and a newer scheme, Schnorr signatures, is standardised for the same curve (Wuille et al., 2020).

Three misunderstandings are common. The first is that signing hides the transaction, which it does not. The second is that the public key could be used to recover the private key, which the one-way property rules out for the computers and algorithms of today (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The third is that the one-way property has been proved: the book says only that the reverse calculation is infeasible with today's computers and algorithms (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), which is a statement about the present state of knowledge and not a mathematical theorem.

nodes.definition: Public key cryptography lets a private key produce a signature that anyone can check against the public key, which is what Bitcoin uses it for, not for encrypting transactions.

nodes.label: Digital signature
nodes.body: A digital signature is a number that a signer computes from a message and from a private key. Anyone who has the message, the signature and the matching public key can verify the signature, that is, can check that it was produced by the holder of the private key and that the message has not been altered since. The book describes this as the central benefit of asymmetric cryptography for Bitcoin: the signature can only be produced by someone with knowledge of the private key, yet it can be verified by anyone with the public key and the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A digital signature is a number that a signer computes from a message and from a private key. Anyone who has the message, the signature and the matching public key can verify the signature, that is, can check that it was produced by the holder of the private key and that the message has not been altered since. The book describes this as the central benefit of asymmetric cryptography for Bitcoin: the signature can only be produced by someone with knowledge of the private key, yet it can be verified by anyone with the public key and the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The signature is how Bitcoin answers the question of who may spend. A transaction input does not carry a name or a password; it carries a signature that proves that the spender controls the key to which the earlier output was paid, as Chapter 2 already noted. Because verification needs only public information, every full node can check every signature independently, which is what lets thousands of nodes that do not know each other agree on which spends are valid.

In Bitcoin the signature is used in every spend of an output that is locked to a key. In the earliest form of payment, which later sections describe, the output script asks for a signature that matches a public key, and the check is carried out by a single operation of the script language. Outside Bitcoin, the same mechanism signs documents, software and web certificates.

The scheme that Bitcoin has traditionally used is the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, ECDSA, over the secp256k1 curve with SHA256 hashes, and a signature is encoded in a variable-size format of up to 72 bytes (Wuille et al., 2020). The chapter's toolkit contains a teaching sketch of the algorithm: given a private key, a message hash and a nonce, which is a one-time secret number, it produces a pair of numbers, and a verifier that knows only the public key accepts the pair for that message hash. The same pair is rejected for a message hash that differs in a single unit, which is the property that ties a signature to one particular transaction. Bitcoin's newer Schnorr signatures use a fixed 64-byte format and a 32-byte public key (Wuille et al., 2020).

A signature scheme is only as good as its handling of the one-time number that goes into every signature. The sketch in the toolkit takes the nonce as an argument so that its output is reproducible; a real signer must derive it deterministically or draw it from a secure random source, and the toolkit says plainly that it is not for use with real funds. ECDSA signatures are also malleable: if a pair of numbers is a valid signature, then the pair with the second number replaced by the group order minus that number is also valid for the same key and message, which Bitcoin handles with a policy rule on the network (Wuille et al., 2020). One of the stated motivations of the segregated witness upgrade, described in its own section, is that signature data no longer takes part in the transaction identifier, so that changes to how a transaction was signed no longer change its identity (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

nodes.label: Private key
nodes.body: A private key is simply a number, picked at random. Control over the private key is the root of user control over all funds associated with the corresponding public key: the key is used to create the signatures that spend bitcoins by proving control of the funds used in a transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's example private key, written in hexadecimal, is 1E99423A4ED27608A15A2616A2B0E9E52CED330AC530EDCC32C8FFC6A526AEDD, which is 256 bits shown as 64 hexadecimal digits of 4 bits each (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A private key is simply a number, picked at random. Control over the private key is the root of user control over all funds associated with the corresponding public key: the key is used to create the signatures that spend bitcoins by proving control of the funds used in a transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's example private key, written in hexadecimal, is 1E99423A4ED27608A15A2616A2B0E9E52CED330AC530EDCC32C8FFC6A526AEDD, which is 256 bits shown as 64 hexadecimal digits of 4 bits each (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Everything else in the system is derived from this one number. The public key, the addresses and the signatures follow from it, while it cannot be recovered from them. That asymmetry makes the private key both the most valuable and the most dangerous secret a Bitcoin user has: whoever learns it can spend the funds, and whoever loses it cannot get them back. The book states both consequences directly, that revealing the key is equivalent to giving control to a third party and that a lost key cannot be recovered (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The private key is met in wallet software, usually out of sight. Chapter 1 explained that a wallet may derive its keys from a recovery code, and later sections of this chapter show the private key written in other formats, such as the wallet import format used to move a key between wallets. A simple tip in the book makes the nature of the key tangible: tossing a coin 256 times gives the binary digits of a random private key that could be used in a Bitcoin wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Not every 256-bit number is a valid key. The private key can be any number between 0 and n minus 1, where n is a constant slightly less than 2 to the 256, defined as the order of the elliptic curve that Bitcoin uses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The constant is FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEBAAEDCE6AF48A03BBFD25E8CD0364141 in hexadecimal (Certicom Research, 2010). Software therefore picks a random 256-bit number and checks that it is less than n, and tries again otherwise. The chance of having to retry is the share of 256-bit numbers that are not below n, about 3.7 times 10 to the minus 39. A key of zero would be useless, because zero times the generator point is the point at infinity and not a public key, so a usable key lies between 1 and n minus 1.

Two details deserve attention. The book prints n as 1.1578 times 10 to the 77, but computing the constant from the standard gives 1.1579 to five significant figures; the difference is a slip in the book's rounding and has no practical consequence. The second detail matters a great deal: any process that is less than completely random can significantly reduce the security of the key and of the bitcoins it controls (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The key space is enormous, about 10 to the 77 numbers, compared with the roughly 10 to the 80 atoms that the book mentions for the visible universe, but that size protects only a key that was chosen without bias.

nodes.definition: A private key is a number picked at random between 1 and n minus 1, where n, about 1.1579 times 10 to the 77, is the order of the curve and slightly less than 2 to the 256.

nodes.label: Public key
nodes.body: A public key is the number, in fact a point on an elliptic curve, that is calculated from a private key and can be shared with anyone. In the book's notation the private key is k, the public key is K, and the relation is K = k times G, where G is a constant point called the generator point (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For the book's example private key the public key is the point whose two coordinates are x = F028892BAD7ED57D2FB57BF33081D5CFCF6F9ED3D3D7F159C2E2FFF579DC341A and y = 07CF33DA18BD734C600B96A72BBC4749D5141C90EC8AC328AE52DDFE2E505BDB (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A public key is the number, in fact a point on an elliptic curve, that is calculated from a private key and can be shared with anyone. In the book's notation the private key is k, the public key is K, and the relation is K = k times G, where G is a constant point called the generator point (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For the book's example private key the public key is the point whose two coordinates are x = F028892BAD7ED57D2FB57BF33081D5CFCF6F9ED3D3D7F159C2E2FFF579DC341A and y = 07CF33DA18BD734C600B96A72BBC4749D5141C90EC8AC328AE52DDFE2E505BDB (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The public key is what lets the rest of the world check a signature without being able to forge one. Because the generator point is the same for every Bitcoin user, a given private key always produces the same public key, and because the calculation cannot be run backwards, the public key does not reveal the private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book summarises this in a tip: a private key can be converted into a public key, but a public key cannot be converted back into a private key, because the math only works one way.

In the earliest design a public key was placed directly in an output script, and Bob would hand his public key to Alice. The book points out that this is impractical, since the key is long: imagine Bob reading the two 64-digit coordinates to Alice over the phone (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Most of the later sections of this chapter, compressed keys, hashed commitments and addresses, exist to solve exactly that practical problem.

The calculation is an elliptic curve multiplication, described in its own section. Software computes K from k by repeated doubling and adding of points, and many Bitcoin implementations delegate the work to the libsecp256k1 library (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The result is a pair of 256-bit coordinates, which can be written in several encodings. The chapter's toolkit reproduces the book's coordinates from the book's private key, and it confirms that the point satisfies the curve equation. The parity of y, odd for the example key, decides whether the compressed encoding starts with 02 or 03, as the compressed key section explains.

A public key is public only in the sense that it can be shared, not in the sense that it must be published early. Bitcoin addresses hide the public key behind a hash until the key is used to spend, and the book's later sections explain what is gained by that. Do not confuse the public key with the address: they are related, but the address is derived from the public key by further steps and has its own formats.

nodes.definition: A public key is the point K = k x G obtained by multiplying the generator point by the private key, which is easy in one direction and infeasible to reverse.

nodes.label: Randomness
nodes.body: Randomness is the property of a number or a sequence of numbers that nobody can predict or repeat. The first and most important step in generating keys is to find a secure source of it, which computer scientists call entropy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word describes both the quality that is needed and, loosely, the material from which random numbers are made.

paras.text: Randomness is the property of a number or a sequence of numbers that nobody can predict or repeat. The first and most important step in generating keys is to find a secure source of it, which computer scientists call entropy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word describes both the quality that is needed and, loosely, the material from which random numbers are made.

A private key protects funds only to the extent that an attacker cannot guess it. A key chosen from a source that is predictable, repeatable or biased may be guessed in far fewer attempts than the size of the key space suggests, even though the key itself looks like an arbitrary 64-digit number. For that reason the source of the number matters more than the number.

Secure randomness works by gathering unpredictability from the physical world and then stretching it. The operating system collects events whose exact timing nobody can reproduce - the intervals between interrupts, the arrival of network packets, the noise of a dedicated hardware source - and mixes them into a pool. A program then asks the system for bytes, and the system returns the output of a cryptographic generator seeded from that pool, which is indistinguishable from random to anyone who does not know the seed. Two consequences matter for a learner. The amount of genuine unpredictability is a property of the seed, not of the length of the output, so stretching 128 bits of entropy into 256 bits of key leaves 128 bits of real strength. And because the quality lives in the system rather than in the arithmetic, the book's rule - use the cryptographically secure generator and do not write your own - is advice about which door to knock on rather than about which formula to use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets the distinction in the standard library of almost any language, which offers two generators side by side: one made for simulations, fast and deliberately reproducible from a seed, and one made for secrets, which cannot be reseeded by the caller and so cannot be replayed. Python names them in just that way, and its documentation says outright that the reproducible one must not be used for security (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The same distinction appears in this chapter's own visual for the concept, where four thousand keys drawn from the reproducible generator are sorted by their first digit: the bars are level, which is what a usable generator looks like, and the picture is identical on every build because the draw was seeded on purpose.

The failures here are historical rather than hypothetical, and they share a shape: the arithmetic was correct and the source was not. A generator seeded from the clock, a generator that restarts from the same state after a reboot, a generator whose output is derived from a passphrase a person invented - each produces keys that look like arbitrary sixty-four-digit numbers and that an attacker can search in a tiny fraction of the key space. A learner should take from this that the size of the key space is an upper bound on security and never a measurement of it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Entropy
nodes.body: Entropy, in the sense the book uses the word, is the unpredictability of the material from which a random number is made, and it is counted in bits. Each fair coin toss that nobody can foresee contributes one bit, so the book's tip that 256 tosses give the binary digits of a random private key is a statement about 256 bits of entropy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The phrase 'cryptographically secure random number generators to produce 256 bits of entropy' describes the practice of Bitcoin software (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Entropy, in the sense the book uses the word, is the unpredictability of the material from which a random number is made, and it is counted in bits. Each fair coin toss that nobody can foresee contributes one bit, so the book's tip that 256 tosses give the binary digits of a random private key is a statement about 256 bits of entropy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The phrase 'cryptographically secure random number generators to produce 256 bits of entropy' describes the practice of Bitcoin software (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The count of bits is the count of equally likely possibilities an attacker would have to try. A source with 256 bits of entropy offers 2 to the 256 possibilities, a number with 78 decimal digits and about 10 to the 77 in size, as the book puts it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). If a program claims to produce a 256-bit key but draws it from a source with only 32 bits of entropy, an attacker faces about four billion possibilities and not 10 to the 77, and the key is weak whatever it looks like.

Entropy is met under several names. Chapter 1 explained that a wallet's recovery code is the basis of its keys and gave the initial entropy of the standard recovery words as 128 to 256 bits, and the Python documentation points to the same idea when it says that the secrets module provides access to the most secure source of randomness that the operating system provides (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Entropy is not generated by a clever formula. A formula can only stretch entropy that already exists, which is what a pseudorandom number generator does when it expands a short seed into a long stream. Therefore the question for any key generator is where its seed comes from. The book's recipe collects a larger string of random bits from a cryptographically secure source and feeds it to SHA256, which conveniently produces a 256-bit value that can be read as a number; if the number is below n it is a suitable private key, and otherwise the process repeats with fresh randomness (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

High-quality-looking output does not prove high entropy. A number that passes casual inspection can come from a seed as small as the current time, and such a key can be found by an attacker who simply tries all plausible seeds, a search of a few million tries rather than the 10 to the 77 that the size of the key space suggests. Nor can the amount of entropy in a number be measured by looking at the number: two keys that look equally arbitrary may have been drawn from sources that differ by seventy orders of magnitude. Treat entropy as a property of the source and never of the printed result, and ask of any key generator where its seed came from.

nodes.definition: Entropy is unpredictability measured in bits; a private key needs 256 bits of it, as many as 256 fair coin tosses supply.

nodes.label: Secure randomness
nodes.body: Secure randomness is what a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator, abbreviated CSPRNG, delivers: numbers that cannot be predicted by an attacker even when the attacker has seen earlier output. The book's warning on the subject is categorical. Do not write your own code to create a random number and do not use a simple random number generator offered by your programming language; use a CSPRNG with a seed from a source of sufficient entropy, and study the documentation of the library you choose to make sure that it is cryptographically secure, because correct implementation of the CSPRNG is critical to the security of the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Secure randomness is what a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator, abbreviated CSPRNG, delivers: numbers that cannot be predicted by an attacker even when the attacker has seen earlier output. The book's warning on the subject is categorical. Do not write your own code to create a random number and do not use a simple random number generator offered by your programming language; use a CSPRNG with a seed from a source of sufficient entropy, and study the documentation of the library you choose to make sure that it is cryptographically secure, because correct implementation of the CSPRNG is critical to the security of the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The warning exists because ordinary generators are designed for a different job. The Python documentation says that the default generator of its random module is designed for modelling and simulation, not for security or cryptography (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Such a generator is a fixed procedure that starts from a seed, so anyone who learns or guesses the seed can reproduce every number that follows. For a private key that is fatal: a key is only as secret as its generator is unpredictable.

Every serious programming environment offers both kinds of generator, and the difference is visible in their documentation. The documentation of Python's secrets module says that the module is used for generating cryptographically strong random numbers suitable for managing data such as passwords, account authentication and security tokens, and that it should be used in preference to the default generator of the random module, which is designed for modelling and simulation, not security or cryptography (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A CSPRNG gathers entropy from the operating system, mixes it and expands it into as many unpredictable bits as are asked for. In Python the call secrets.randbelow(m) returns a random integer from 0 up to but not including m, drawn from the most secure source the operating system provides (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Choosing a key with it takes one line: ask for a number below n minus 1 and add 1, which yields a number from 1 to n minus 1. The default generator of the random module, by contrast, is repeatable on purpose: two generators started from the same seed give the same number, a property that the chapter's checks confirm and that is useful for experiments and disastrous for keys.

Following the rule requires attention to details that are easy to overlook. A generator that is secure in principle can be misused by seeding it with a poor value, by calling it before the system has gathered enough entropy, or by running it on a machine whose random source is compromised. Keys should be generated on a device that you control, and the quality of the software should not be taken on trust. The book names generating code that is compromised with a back door as one of the pitfalls of paper wallets, a subject that a later section returns to (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: A private key must come from a cryptographically secure random generator; Python's secrets module is documented for that use and its random module for modelling and simulation.

nodes.label: The curve
nodes.body: The curve is the mathematical object on which Bitcoin's public key cryptography is built. Elliptic curve cryptography, abbreviated ECC, is a type of asymmetric or public key cryptography based on the discrete logarithm problem as expressed by addition and multiplication on the points of an elliptic curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This level of the chapter gathers everything that is needed to understand that sentence: the arithmetic of a finite field, the curve itself, the way points are added, the particular curve that Bitcoin uses and the standard that defines it, the generator point, multiplication of a point by a number, and the problem that makes the whole construction hard to reverse.

paras.text: The curve is the mathematical object on which Bitcoin's public key cryptography is built. Elliptic curve cryptography, abbreviated ECC, is a type of asymmetric or public key cryptography based on the discrete logarithm problem as expressed by addition and multiplication on the points of an elliptic curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This level of the chapter gathers everything that is needed to understand that sentence: the arithmetic of a finite field, the curve itself, the way points are added, the particular curve that Bitcoin uses and the standard that defines it, the generator point, multiplication of a point by a number, and the problem that makes the whole construction hard to reverse.

A reader who only wants to use Bitcoin can treat the conversion from private key to public key as a black box, but a reader who wants to judge the security of Bitcoin cannot. Every claim of the form 'the public key does not reveal the private key' rests on the properties of this one curve. The book therefore spends a section on it, and it notes that the math is identical whether the curve is drawn over the real numbers, shown over a small finite field or taken over the enormous field that Bitcoin uses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The construction works in three layers, each built from the one below. The bottom layer is a finite field: the numbers are the remainders after division by one very large prime, and addition and multiplication are the ordinary operations followed by taking the remainder, which keeps every result inside the same finite set. The middle layer is the curve, the set of pairs in that field satisfying the curve's equation, together with one extra point that acts as a zero. On that set an addition of points is defined geometrically - draw the line through two points, take the third point where it meets the curve, reflect it - and the definition turns the curve into a group, which is the only property the cryptography needs. The top layer is multiplication of a point by a whole number, which is repeated addition carried out by doubling, so that a multiplier of two hundred and fifty-six bits costs a few hundred operations rather than astronomically many. A public key is the generator point multiplied by the private key, and the discrete logarithm problem is the absence of any comparable shortcut in the other direction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Certicom Research, 2010).

The reader meets this level twice over, at two scales. The small scale is the chapter's own worked examples over the field with seventeen elements, where the whole curve has few enough points to list and a student can check an addition on paper; the arithmetic there is identical to the arithmetic Bitcoin uses, which is the point of showing it. The large scale is the curve named in the standard, whose parameters this chapter quotes from the specification and whose generator point it encodes; the same parameters are what the library inside every wallet is compiled with (Certicom Research, 2010) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Two cautions about pictures and about proofs. The smooth curve drawn in textbooks over the real numbers is a teaching aid: over a finite field the points are a scatter with no shape to the eye, and a learner who reasons from the drawing will reach wrong conclusions about how many points lie near one another. And the hardness of the discrete logarithm problem is not a theorem but the present state of the art; no proof exists that no shortcut can be found, so every statement about the strength of a key in this chapter is a statement about what is known today (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Finite field
nodes.body: A finite field of prime order p, written F_p, is the set of whole numbers from 0 to p minus 1 together with the four arithmetic operations, in which every result is replaced by its remainder after division by p. The book writes the remainder operation as 'mod p' and says that it indicates that the curve is over a finite field of prime order p (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because the remainder always lies between 0 and p minus 1, the numbers never grow beyond the size of p, and every non-zero number has a partner by which it can be multiplied to give 1.

paras.text: A finite field of prime order p, written F_p, is the set of whole numbers from 0 to p minus 1 together with the four arithmetic operations, in which every result is replaced by its remainder after division by p. The book writes the remainder operation as 'mod p' and says that it indicates that the curve is over a finite field of prime order p (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because the remainder always lies between 0 and p minus 1, the numbers never grow beyond the size of p, and every non-zero number has a partner by which it can be multiplied to give 1.

The elliptic curve of Bitcoin is defined over a finite field instead of over the real numbers, and this choice is what makes it usable in software. Real numbers have to be rounded by a computer, whereas arithmetic modulo a prime is exact. The price is that the curve no longer looks like a smooth line. The book remarks that because the curve is defined over a finite field of prime order, it looks like a pattern of dots scattered in two dimensions, which makes it difficult to visualise, although the math is identical to that of an elliptic curve over real numbers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Modular arithmetic is met outside cryptography as well, in clocks, in check digits and in the checksums of this chapter's later sections. In Bitcoin it appears whenever a coordinate of a point is calculated, and the prime in question is p = 2 to the 256 minus 2 to the 32 minus 2 to the 9 minus 2 to the 8 minus 2 to the 7 minus 2 to the 6 minus 2 to the 4 minus 1, a very large prime number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard gives the same prime in hexadecimal, as FFFFFFFF followed by repeated groups of F and ending in FFFFFC2F, and in the same long form (Certicom Research, 2010). Written more briefly it is 2 to the 256 minus 2 to the 32 minus 977, an equality that the chapter's checks verify.

In Python the operator % gives the remainder, and pow(a, -1, p) gives the number by which a must be multiplied, modulo p, to obtain 1. In the field with 17 elements the partner of 5 is 7, because 5 times 7 is 35 and 35 leaves the remainder 1 when divided by 17; the chapter's checks confirm that every number from 1 to 16 has such a partner. Division by a is defined as multiplication by its partner. That operation, the modular inverse, is what the slope calculation in point addition needs, and the toolkit of this chapter uses exactly this call to add points on the real curve.

A finite field is not a number line, so ordinary intuitions about size and order fail: 16 is not 'greater' than 1 in any useful sense once results wrap around. The prime matters, too. A probabilistic primality test confirms that Bitcoin's p is prime, and with a modulus that is not prime some numbers would have no inverse. Finally, remember that p is only slightly smaller than 2 to the 256, the size of a private key, but it is a different number from n, the order of the curve; the two are easily confused.

nodes.definition: A finite field of prime order p is the whole numbers from 0 to p - 1 with addition, subtraction, multiplication and division carried out modulo p; division by 5 modulo 17 is multiplication by 7.

nodes.label: Elliptic curve
nodes.body: An elliptic curve is the set of all points (x, y) whose coordinates satisfy an equation of a particular form, together with one extra point called the point at infinity. The curve of Bitcoin has the equation y squared = x cubed + 7, which the book writes as y squared mod p = (x cubed + 7) mod p because the arithmetic is carried out in a finite field (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the notation of the standard the equation is y squared = x cubed + ax + b, and for this curve a is 0 and b is 7 (Certicom Research, 2010).

paras.text: An elliptic curve is the set of all points (x, y) whose coordinates satisfy an equation of a particular form, together with one extra point called the point at infinity. The curve of Bitcoin has the equation y squared = x cubed + 7, which the book writes as y squared mod p = (x cubed + 7) mod p because the arithmetic is carried out in a finite field (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the notation of the standard the equation is y squared = x cubed + ax + b, and for this curve a is 0 and b is 7 (Certicom Research, 2010).

The reason for choosing such a curve is that its points can be added to one another by a simple rule, so that the points form a system on which multiplication by a whole number is easy to compute and its inverse is believed hard. Those two properties together give Bitcoin its one-way function. The curve is not valuable for its shape but for the algebra that its points obey.

Over the real numbers the curve is a smooth line, drawn in the book as a figure that is symmetric about the x-axis, which is to say that it is reflected like a mirror by the axis (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Over a finite field it becomes a scatter of dots on a grid. The book shows the same equation over the field with 17 elements, and the chapter's checks find that it has exactly 17 points whose coordinates are whole numbers from 0 to 16, which together with the point at infinity makes 18. Bitcoin's own curve is, in the book's words, a much more complex pattern of dots on an unfathomably large grid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

To check that a point lies on the curve you substitute its coordinates into the equation. The book gives a point P with two 77-digit coordinates and shows in Python that x cubed plus 7 minus y squared leaves the remainder 0 when divided by p, so the point is on the curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the chapter's checks reproduce that result. A point whose coordinates do not give 0 is not a valid public key. For every point (x, y) on the curve the point (x, minus y) is also on the curve, which is the symmetry about the x-axis in the finite world: in the field with 17 elements the point (1, 5) has the mirror image (1, 12), since 17 minus 5 is 12.

The word 'elliptic' is misleading, because the curve is not an ellipse. Do not take the smooth picture literally for Bitcoin, either: it explains the geometry of addition, but the real curve has only whole-number points modulo p and the lines of the drawing do not exist there. The book is careful on this point and says that the math is the same, which is why the drawing remains a faithful guide (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: An elliptic curve is the set of points (x, y) that satisfy an equation such as y squared = x cubed + 7, together with a point at infinity; over the field with 17 elements the curve y squared = x cubed + 7 has 17 points besides the point at infinity.

nodes.label: Point addition and the point at infinity
nodes.body: Point addition is the operation by which two points of an elliptic curve are combined into a third point of the same curve. Given two points P1 and P2, there is a third point P3 = P1 + P2, also on the curve; the book describes it geometrically: draw a line between P1 and P2, which will intersect the curve in exactly one additional place, call that point P3' = (x, y), and then reflect it in the x-axis to get P3 = (x, minus y) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The curve also contains the point at infinity, which roughly corresponds to the role of zero in addition.

paras.text: Point addition is the operation by which two points of an elliptic curve are combined into a third point of the same curve. Given two points P1 and P2, there is a third point P3 = P1 + P2, also on the curve; the book describes it geometrically: draw a line between P1 and P2, which will intersect the curve in exactly one additional place, call that point P3' = (x, y), and then reflect it in the x-axis to get P3 = (x, minus y) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The curve also contains the point at infinity, which roughly corresponds to the role of zero in addition.

Addition is the only operation that has to be defined, because everything else in elliptic curve cryptography is built from it. Multiplication of a point is repeated addition, the public key is such a multiple, and the verification of a signature adds points. That the rule yields a third point of the curve, and not a point somewhere else in the plane, is what makes the curve a closed system. The book adds that the addition is associative, so that A + B + C can be written without parentheses and without ambiguity (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

In the field with 17 elements the points of the curve y squared = x cubed + 7 can be added by hand. Adding (1, 5) and (2, 7) gives (1, 12). Adding (1, 5) to itself gives (2, 10). Adding (1, 5) and (1, 12), two points with the same x value and different y values, gives the point at infinity. Adding the point at infinity to any point gives that point back. The chapter's checks confirm each of these sums and also the associativity rule on an example; they use the same rules that the toolkit applies to the big curve.

There are special cases, and the book explains why they require the point at infinity. If P1 and P2 are the same point, the line between them is replaced by the tangent to the curve at that point, which intersects the curve in exactly one new point; the techniques of calculus find its slope, and they work even though the points have whole-number coordinates. If P1 and P2 have the same x value but different y values, the line is vertical and the result is the point at infinity. If P1 is the point at infinity, then P1 + P2 = P2, and the same holds with the roles exchanged, which shows how the point at infinity plays the role of zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In software the point at infinity is sometimes represented by x = y = 0, which does not satisfy the curve equation but is an easy separate case to check for (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The formulas that software uses are algebraic, not geometric, and they work in the finite field with modular division, so the picture of a line crossing a curve must not be taken literally. The chapter's toolkit shows the cost of care: each case, doubling, inverse points and the point at infinity, needs its own branch, and a mistake in one of them produces points that are not on the curve and public keys that nobody can use. This is one more reason to rely on a well-tested library in practice.

nodes.definition: Two points of the curve are added by drawing a line through them, finding the third intersection and reflecting it in the x-axis; the point at infinity plays the role of zero.

nodes.label: The secp256k1 curve
nodes.body: The name secp256k1 identifies the specific elliptic curve and the set of constants that Bitcoin uses. The curve is y squared = x cubed + 7 over a finite field of prime order p, with p = 2 to the 256 minus 2 to the 32 minus 2 to the 9 minus 2 to the 8 minus 2 to the 7 minus 2 to the 6 minus 2 to the 4 minus 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard that defines it specifies the parameters as a sextuple of the prime p, the coefficients a and b, the base point G, the order n of G and the cofactor h, which the standard defines as the number of points of the curve divided by n; for secp256k1 the coefficient a is 0, the coefficient b is 7 and the cofactor is 1, which means that the points of the curve are exactly the multiples of G (Certicom Research, 2010).

The curve is y squared = x cubed + 7 over a finite field of prime order p, with p = 2 to the 256 minus 2 to the 32 minus 2 to the 9 minus 2 to the 8 minus 2 to the 7 minus 2 to the 6 minus 2 to the 4 minus 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard that defines it specifies the parameters as a sextuple of the prime p, the coefficients a and b, the base point G, the order n of G and the cofactor h, which the standard defines as the number of points of the curve divided by n; for secp256k1 the coefficient a is 0, the coefficient b is 7 and the cofactor is 1, which means that the points of the curve are exactly the multiples of G (Certicom Research, 2010).

Every Bitcoin public key is a point on this one curve, and every Bitcoin signature is checked against it. Fixing a single curve and a single generator point means that all participants perform the same calculation and obtain the same answer from the same private key. The choice also fixes the security level: the standard's table of properties gives secp256k1 a security strength of 128 bits for a field size of 256 bits (Certicom Research, 2010), and that figure, not the 256 bits of the key itself, is the amount of work an attacker is estimated to need.

The name is met in the documentation of every Bitcoin library, in the title of the Schnorr signature standard, which is called Schnorr Signatures for secp256k1 (Wuille et al., 2020), and in the book's remark that Bitcoin uses a specific curve and set of constants as defined in a standard called secp256k1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The name is also a small code. In the words of the standard, each name begins with sec to denote Standards for Efficient Cryptography, followed by p to denote parameters over a prime field, a number for the length in bits of the field size, a k for parameters associated with a Koblitz curve or an r for verifiably random parameters, and a sequence number (Certicom Research, 2010).

To use the curve in a program one needs only p, the generator G and the order n. The chapter's checks verify the book's example point P against the equation, compute p from its short form, and confirm that the generator point lies on the curve and that adding it to itself n times gives the point at infinity. They also parse the constants from the standard's text and compare them with the toolkit's constants, so that the numbers used in this chapter are the standard's and not copies from memory.

One statement in the book does not match its source. The book says that secp256k1 was established by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, but the curve is defined in SEC 2, Standards for Efficient Cryptography, published by Certicom Research in 2010, and the status table in that document marks secp256k1 with a dash in the NIST column, meaning not conformant with the NIST list, while secp256r1 is marked r, explicitly recommended (Certicom Research, 2010). The error is easy to repeat and matters when a reader is asked whether Bitcoin's curve was chosen by a government agency: according to the standard it is not one of the curves on the NIST list.

nodes.label: Curve standard (SEC 2 and NIST)
nodes.body: A curve standard is a published document that fixes the constants of an elliptic curve so that independent programmers obtain the same curve. The standard behind Bitcoin is SEC 2, Recommended Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters, version 2.0, published on 27 January 2010 by Certicom Research under the name Standards for Efficient Cryptography (Certicom Research, 2010). It lists recommended parameters over prime fields in several sizes, from 192 to 521 bits, and gives each set of parameters a nickname such as secp256k1 or secp256r1.

paras.text: A curve standard is a published document that fixes the constants of an elliptic curve so that independent programmers obtain the same curve. The standard behind Bitcoin is SEC 2, Recommended Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters, version 2.0, published on 27 January 2010 by Certicom Research under the name Standards for Efficient Cryptography (Certicom Research, 2010). It lists recommended parameters over prime fields in several sizes, from 192 to 521 bits, and gives each set of parameters a nickname such as secp256k1 or secp256r1.

A curve is not safe merely because it has a name. Choosing the coefficients and the generator point is a decision that the user of the curve cannot check without help, which is why standards distinguish between parameters associated with a Koblitz curve, marked k, and parameters chosen verifiably at random, marked r (Certicom Research, 2010). The standard also records how each set of parameters aligns with other standards, which tells a reader who else supports the curve and who recommends it.

The alignment table is Table 2 of the document. Its columns name other standards: ANSI X9.62, ANSI X9.63, echeck, IEEE P1363, IPSec, NIST and WAP. A dash denotes parameters not conformant with the standard of that column, the letter c denotes conformant parameters and the letter r denotes parameters explicitly recommended in the standard (Certicom Research, 2010). In the NIST column secp256k1 has a dash and secp256r1 has an r, which is the evidence for the correction in the previous concept. The chapter's checks read the table rows from the text of the standard.

To trace a curve to its source, one starts from the name and looks for its section in the standard. Section 2.4.1 specifies secp256k1 and section 2.4.2 specifies secp256r1 (Certicom Research, 2010). The parameters appear as hexadecimal numbers, and the prime p is also given as 2 to the 256 minus 2 to the 32 minus 2 to the 9 minus 2 to the 8 minus 2 to the 7 minus 2 to the 6 minus 2 to the 4 minus 1, the form the book uses. Anyone implementing the curve can check a copy of the constants against this text.

A standards document is a draft or a version at a given date, and the table reflects the status at that date. SEC 2 version 2.0 labels itself a draft in its page headers, so statements about 'the NIST list' should be read as statements about the list that the document refers to. When a textbook and a primary document disagree, the primary document is the better evidence for what it says itself, and the discrepancy is worth reporting rather than silently correcting.

nodes.definition: SEC 2 lists recommended curve parameters with a table of which other standards each conforms to; secp256k1 is marked as not on the NIST list and secp256r1 is marked as recommended by it.

nodes.label: Generator point
nodes.body: The generator point, written G, is the predetermined point on the curve by which a private key is multiplied to give the public key. It is specified as part of the secp256k1 standard and is always the same for all keys in Bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard gives it in compressed form as 02 followed by the x coordinate 79BE667EF9DCBBAC55A06295CE870B07029BFCDB2DCE28D959F2815B16F81798, and in uncompressed form as 04 followed by that x coordinate and a y coordinate of 256 bits (Certicom Research, 2010).

paras.text: The generator point, written G, is the predetermined point on the curve by which a private key is multiplied to give the public key. It is specified as part of the secp256k1 standard and is always the same for all keys in Bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard gives it in compressed form as 02 followed by the x coordinate 79BE667EF9DCBBAC55A06295CE870B07029BFCDB2DCE28D959F2815B16F81798, and in uncompressed form as 04 followed by that x coordinate and a y coordinate of 256 bits (Certicom Research, 2010).

Because the generator point is the same for every Bitcoin user, a private key k multiplied by G will always result in the same public key K (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That uniqueness lets any two programs agree on the public key without exchanging any information about it. The same property is what lets this chapter's toolkit reproduce the public key that the book prints for its example private key.

The generator appears wherever a public key is derived from a private key and wherever a signature is verified. The book pictures the process as starting from G and doubling it: its figure shows G, 2G and 4G as a geometric operation on the curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the standard, G is paired with n, the order of G, and a cofactor h of 1, the ratio between the number of points of the curve and n, which says that the curve holds no points besides the multiples of G (Certicom Research, 2010).

The order n is the number of times G must be added to itself to arrive at the point at infinity. The chapter's checks confirm for the standard's n that n times G is the point at infinity, that n minus 1 times G is the mirror image of G, and that n is prime. The first of these facts means that private keys beyond n minus 1 would only repeat earlier public keys, which is why the valid private keys are the numbers from 1 to n minus 1. The second says that the multiples of G form a loop of exactly n members, of which the public keys are the members other than the point at infinity.

The generator is public and standard, so it contributes nothing to secrecy; the secrecy is entirely in the multiplier. A reader should also not confuse the generator point G with the base point of a different curve, nor with a public key: G is a constant of the standard, while a public key is a multiple of G chosen by a private key.

nodes.example: G, the same for every key
nodes.definition: The generator point G is the fixed point of the secp256k1 standard from which every public key is reached by multiplication; adding it to itself n times gives the point at infinity.
