nodes.label: Elliptic curve multiplication
nodes.body: Elliptic curve multiplication takes a point P and a whole number k and produces kP, which is defined as P + P + P + ... + P with k terms. The book defines multiplication in the standard way that extends addition, and notes that k is sometimes confusingly called an exponent in this case (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Bitcoin the point is the generator point and the multiplier is the private key, so the public key is K = k times G.

paras.text: Elliptic curve multiplication takes a point P and a whole number k and produces kP, which is defined as P + P + P + ... + P with k terms. The book defines multiplication in the standard way that extends addition, and notes that k is sometimes confusingly called an exponent in this case (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Bitcoin the point is the generator point and the multiplier is the private key, so the public key is K = k times G.

This single operation is the heart of Bitcoin's cryptography. It is easy in one direction and impossible, for any practical purpose, to reverse: the book calls it a trap door function, which is easy to do in one direction, multiplication, and impossible to do in the reverse direction, division (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Someone with a private key can easily create the public key and share it knowing that no one can reverse the function and calculate the private key from the public key; the same trick makes unforgeable digital signatures possible.

The book illustrates multiplication on the curve over the real numbers: adding a point to itself corresponds to drawing the tangent at the point, finding where it intersects the curve again, and reflecting that point in the x-axis, and its figure shows G, 2G and 4G obtained this way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In real software the multiplication is performed by a library, such as libsecp256k1, which many Bitcoin implementations use for the elliptic curve math (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Adding G to itself k times, where k is a 256-bit number, would be impossible. The double-and-add method avoids it by reading the bits of k. Starting from the leading bit, the method doubles the running point for every further bit and adds P whenever the bit is 1. For the book's example key, which has 253 bits of which 124 are set, this means 252 doublings and 123 additions, a few hundred operations instead of an astronomically large number; the chapter's checks compute these counts and verify that the toolkit's result for this key matches the public key printed in the book. They also check that (a + b) times G equals aG plus bG for sample multipliers, which is the algebraic law the method relies on.

Multiplication is the fast direction only. The reverse calculation, finding k when K is known, is the discrete logarithm problem described in the next concept. Also do not confuse point multiplication with multiplying two points, which is not defined: the multiplier is always a plain whole number. Finally, the fact that a short loop of additions suffices for the forward direction does not make the chapter's toolkit safe for real use; its own description says so, and the concept on cryptographic libraries returns to the point.

nodes.definition: Multiplying a point by a whole number k means adding it to itself k times, which the double-and-add method does in about 256 doublings and additions; for the book's key it is 252 doublings and 123 additions.

nodes.label: Discrete logarithm and brute-force search
nodes.body: The discrete logarithm problem asks for the multiplier when the product is known. In elliptic curve terms: given the public key K and the generator point G, find the private key k with K = kG. The book calls this reverse operation 'finding the discrete logarithm' and says that it is as difficult as trying all possible values of k, that is, a brute-force search (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A brute-force search is simply the method of trying every candidate in turn until one fits.

paras.text: The discrete logarithm problem asks for the multiplier when the product is known. In elliptic curve terms: given the public key K and the generator point G, find the private key k with K = kG. The book calls this reverse operation 'finding the discrete logarithm' and says that it is as difficult as trying all possible values of k, that is, a brute-force search (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A brute-force search is simply the method of trying every candidate in turn until one fits.

The whole security of Bitcoin's ownership rule rests on the difficulty of this problem. If anyone could compute k from K, every public key that has ever appeared on the blockchain would reveal its private key, and anyone could spend anyone's coins. This is why the book calls elliptic curve multiplication a one-way function and bases the entire scheme on it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The same pattern of an easy forward step and a hard reverse step occurs in the exponentiation of prime numbers that the book names as another suitable function (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and it can be seen in a small group. In the numbers modulo 101, raising 2 to the power 9 gives 7. Going backwards, from 7 to the exponent 9, requires trying exponents one after another until one fits, and the chapter's check does exactly that and stops at 9. Every step of the forward direction is a single call of pow, while the reverse direction needs a search.

For a private key of 256 bits the number of candidates is about 10 to the 77, far more than any computer could try. The standard's table of properties gives secp256k1 a security strength of 128 bits for a 256-bit field, which it describes as the approximate number of bits of security the parameters offer (Certicom Research, 2010). That figure is half of the 256-bit field size, so the book's statement that the problem is as difficult as brute force over all values of k is best read as a simplification: a search over every key would correspond to 256 bits of security and not 128. The practical conclusion stands either way, because 2 to the 128 operations remain out of reach.

The difficulty of the discrete logarithm is an assumption about the present state of mathematics and computing, not a proved theorem. The book is careful to speak of what is infeasible 'using the computers and algorithms available today' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Reasoning from this assumption, a good habit is to make no stronger claim than the source does, and to keep in mind that the strength of 128 bits holds only if the private key is chosen at random from the full range.

nodes.definition: Finding the multiplier k from K = kG is the discrete logarithm problem; with no shortcut it is as hard as trying every value of k, a brute-force search; in a toy group modulo 101 it takes 9 tries to find that 2 to the power 9 leaves 7.

io.code: next(k for k in range(1, 101) if pow(2, k, 101) == 7)

nodes.label: Cryptographic library (libsecp256k1)
nodes.body: A cryptographic library is a collection of ready-made routines for cryptographic calculations that programs call instead of writing the mathematics themselves. For the elliptic curve math of Bitcoin the book names the libsecp256k1 cryptographic library and observes that many Bitcoin implementations use it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The library carries out the point arithmetic, the multiplication and the signature operations of the curve that this level has just described.

paras.text: A cryptographic library is a collection of ready-made routines for cryptographic calculations that programs call instead of writing the mathematics themselves. For the elliptic curve math of Bitcoin the book names the libsecp256k1 cryptographic library and observes that many Bitcoin implementations use it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The library carries out the point arithmetic, the multiplication and the signature operations of the curve that this level has just described.

Cryptographic code must be exactly right, because an error that passes every ordinary test can still leak a key or accept a forged signature. The book's advice about random numbers shows the attitude: do not write your own code, study the documentation of the library you choose, and remember that correct implementation is critical to the security of the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The authors of the Schnorr signature standard make the same point about verification: to be safe for use in a consensus system, the verification algorithm must be completely specified at the byte level, so that nobody can construct a signature that is valid to some verifiers but not all (Wuille et al., 2020).

The reference implementation of Chapter 3, Bitcoin Core, and the wrapper libraries that call it are the kind of shared software that Bitcoin users rely on; a cryptographic library is the same idea one level lower, below the wallet and the node. When a wallet developer in another language implements a wallet, the library is what ensures that every implementation derives the same public key from the same private key.

The toolkit that accompanies this chapter shows what such a library does. The point addition and multiplication of the curve take thirteen lines of Python, fewer than twenty, and with them the toolkit reproduces the public key of the book's example, the addresses of the later sections and the bech32 examples. Its results were compared with Bitcoin Core 31.1, which gave the same addresses for the same keys, and with the reference code that the book uses for bech32. A library does the same arithmetic with the care that production use demands.

The toolkit is written for reading. Its own description says that it is not for use with real funds, because it is not constant-time, which means that the time it takes depends on the key, and because it takes no care over where randomness comes from. Never copy educational code into a wallet. The comparison with independent software also shows how trust is built in this field: not by believing one implementation, but by checking that several independent ones agree.

nodes.definition: A cryptographic library is tested, reusable code for the elliptic curve math; the book notes that many Bitcoin implementations use libsecp256k1, and this chapter's toolkit is only a readable sketch of the same calculation.

nodes.label: Hash functions
nodes.body: A hash function is the second tool, next to the elliptic curve, from which Bitcoin addresses are built. This level introduces the general idea and the three functions the chapter uses: SHA256, RIPEMD-160 and the combination of the two that Bitcoin calls HASH160. Together they allow a long public key, or a script of thousands of bytes, to be replaced by a short and reliable fingerprint that can be copied, printed and checked.

paras.text: A hash function is the second tool, next to the elliptic curve, from which Bitcoin addresses are built. This level introduces the general idea and the three functions the chapter uses: SHA256, RIPEMD-160 and the combination of the two that Bitcoin calls HASH160. Together they allow a long public key, or a script of thousands of bytes, to be replaced by a short and reliable fingerprint that can be copied, printed and checked.

The book states the practical problem in these terms: Bitcoin already contains several data structures much larger than 65 bytes that need to be securely referenced in other parts of Bitcoin using the smallest amount of data that was secure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A hash function solves the problem of referring to a large object by a small one without losing the guarantee that the reference identifies exactly that object.

A hash function works by consuming its input in fixed-size blocks and stirring each block into a small block of internal state, so that the state at the end depends on every bit of the input and on the order in which the bits arrived. Three properties are what make the result usable as a reference. The output has the same length whatever the input is, so a reference to a short key and a reference to a long script cost the same. Changing any part of the input changes about half the bits of the output, so two inputs that differ slightly have outputs with nothing visibly in common. And the function cannot be run backwards, so a reference can be published without publishing what it refers to - which is exactly what an address does. Chaining two different functions, as Bitcoin does when it applies the second to the output of the first, shortens the result and means that a weakness found in one of them is not on its own a weakness in the pair (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2015).

The reader meets these functions at every step of the chapter and then everywhere else in the course. Here they turn a public key into the twenty bytes an address commits to, and they produce the four checksum bytes that protect the text of the address. In chapter 2 the same arithmetic gave the identifier of a transaction and the root of a block's Merkle tree; in chapter 3 it gave the identifier of a block; in chapter 5 it is the engine of the key-stretching step that turns a recovery code into a seed. The functions themselves are published standards rather than Bitcoin's own, which is why this course quotes a national standard for the first of them (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2015).

The caution is about strength and about length. A hash is only as strong as the shorter of the function and the output: cutting a thirty-two byte result down to twenty bytes, as Bitcoin does, lowers the work an attacker needs, and the three attacks described later in this chapter are the reason the newer addresses commit to thirty-two bytes instead. And one of the two functions used here is no longer available in every current software library, which is why this course states the lengths it produces and cites them to their standard rather than recomputing them in the browser (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Hash function
nodes.body: A hash function is a function that takes a potentially large amount of data, scrambles it (hashes it), and outputs a fixed amount of data. A cryptographic hash function will always produce the same output when given the same input, and a secure function also makes it impractical for somebody to choose a different input that produces a previously seen output (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard that defines the SHA family describes its algorithms as ones that generate digests of messages, which are used to detect whether messages have been changed since the digests were generated (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2015).

paras.text: A hash function is a function that takes a potentially large amount of data, scrambles it (hashes it), and outputs a fixed amount of data. A cryptographic hash function will always produce the same output when given the same input, and a secure function also makes it impractical for somebody to choose a different input that produces a previously seen output (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard that defines the SHA family describes its algorithms as ones that generate digests of messages, which are used to detect whether messages have been changed since the digests were generated (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2015).

These two properties make the output a commitment to the input, which is a promise that, in practice, only input x will produce output X (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book illustrates this with a question whose answer is revealed later: it publishes the hash of its answer now, and after the guess has been made it shows that the answer, put into the hash function, gives exactly the published value. In Bitcoin the same trick lets a receiver publish a small commitment to a public key or a script and reveal the full object only when it is used.

Hash functions occur throughout this book. Chapter 1's proof of work is a search for an input whose hash has a required form, Chapter 3 verified that a downloaded release file has the published hash, and this chapter uses hashes for addresses and for checksums. The program command sha256sum, which the book uses in its example, computes one of them from the command line.

The chapter's checks show the behaviour on the book's own example. The sentence the book hashes, followed by the line break that the echo command adds, has the SHA256 value 94d7a772612c8f2f2ec609d41f5bd3d04a5aa1dfe3582f04af517d396a302e4e, as printed in the book, and the same input gives it every time. Two inputs that differ in a single bit, the letter a and the character just before it in the ASCII table, give outputs that differ in 139 of their 256 bits, a little more than the half that one would expect from an unrelated pair: a tiny change in the input scrambles the output completely, so a near-miss reveals nothing about the right input.

A hash is not an encryption: there is no key and no way to recover the input from the output except by guessing it. For the same reason it is not a good way to hide a small set of possible inputs. If the answer can only be one of a handful of years, anyone can hash all the candidates and compare, so a commitment hides a secret only when the set of possible secrets is huge. Finally, 'secure' is relative to output size: the shorter the output, the easier it is to find collisions, as the discussion of collision attacks later in the chapter shows.

nodes.definition: A hash function takes a potentially large amount of data and outputs a fixed amount of data; a cryptographic hash function always gives the same output for the same input, and changing one bit of the input changes about half of the output bits.

nodes.label: SHA256
nodes.body: SHA256 is the member of the SHA family that produces 256 bits (32 bytes) of output, and the book calls it the function most commonly used in Bitcoin and considers it to be very secure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Its output is less than half the size of the original Bitcoin public keys, which were 65 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the chapter's checks confirm that 32 is smaller than half of 65.

paras.text: SHA256 is the member of the SHA family that produces 256 bits (32 bytes) of output, and the book calls it the function most commonly used in Bitcoin and considers it to be very secure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Its output is less than half the size of the original Bitcoin public keys, which were 65 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the chapter's checks confirm that 32 is smaller than half of 65.

Bitcoin leans on SHA256 for many jobs. This chapter meets it as the first step of HASH160, as the double hash that gives base58check its checksum and as the function the book recommends for turning random bits into a private key candidate. Using one well-studied function in all these places keeps the system simple, and it means that a weakness in it would affect everything at once.

The command-line example in the book uses the tool sha256sum. Python offers the same function in its hashlib module, and the chapter's checks use it throughout. The hashlib module also provides functions of other families, but the Python that runs inside this course's browser pages has no RIPEMD-160, which is why some examples in this chapter are given as data.

The input can have any length and the output always has 32 bytes. The three-byte message abc has the SHA256 digest that begins ba7816bf, and the empty message and a message of a million bytes also give 32 bytes. The chapter's checks print the length for several inputs. Applying the function twice, as base58check does, is simply passing the 32-byte output as the input of a second call.

A 256-bit output does not mean 256 bits of security for every attack. For finding two inputs with the same hash the work is about the square root of the number of outputs, so the best case is 128 bits, and for the 160-bit RIPEMD-160 it is 80 bits; the book's discussion of collision attacks makes exactly this point (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Choose the right function and the right question: preimage resistance, second preimage resistance and collision resistance are three different properties.

nodes.definition: SHA256 is the hash function most commonly used in Bitcoin; its output is 256 bits (32 bytes), and the SHA256 of the three bytes abc begins ba7816bf.

nodes.label: RIPEMD-160
nodes.body: RIPEMD-160 is a hash function whose output is 160 bits (20 bytes). The book describes it as one of the other, slightly less secure hash functions that produce smaller output than SHA256 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Its place in Bitcoin is as the second step of the commitment to a public key, applied to the SHA256 digest of the key.

paras.text: RIPEMD-160 is a hash function whose output is 160 bits (20 bytes). The book describes it as one of the other, slightly less secure hash functions that produce smaller output than SHA256 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Its place in Bitcoin is as the second step of the commitment to a public key, applied to the SHA256 digest of the key.

A smaller output means a shorter address and a smaller transaction. The original version of Bitcoin made commitments to public keys by first hashing the key with SHA256 and then hashing that output with RIPEMD-160, which produced a 20-byte commitment, and the book adds that Satoshi Nakamoto never stated the reasons for this choice (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The honest statement is therefore that the design is known and the motive is not.

RIPEMD-160 is met in Bitcoin in three kinds of place: the 20-byte commitments inside legacy addresses, the 20-byte witness programs of version 0 pay to witness public key hash outputs, and the commitments to scripts in pay to script hash outputs, all of which later sections describe. The checksums of the next branch use SHA256 alone, applied twice.

In Python the call hashlib.new('ripemd160', data) computes it where the underlying library supports the function, and the chapter's checks use it to reproduce the book's addresses. The course's browser pages do not provide it in their Python, so examples that depend on it are given as data there. Because it works on its input in the same way for every call, two parties that apply SHA256 and then RIPEMD-160 to the same public key obtain the same 20 bytes.

The size of the output limits security. The book states that for a secure 160-bit algorithm the chance of independently finding an input for an existing commitment is 1 in 2 to the 160, a preimage attack, but that when an attacker can influence the original input, the strength drops to the square root, 1 in 2 to the 80 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For this reason newer address types use SHA256 alone, which gives commitments of 32 bytes, as the later section on segwit outputs explains.

nodes.definition: RIPEMD-160 is a hash function with a 160-bit (20-byte) output; Bitcoin applies it to the SHA256 of a public key to obtain a 20-byte commitment.

nodes.label: HASH160
nodes.body: HASH160 is the name of the combination RIPEMD160(SHA256(K)), in which a public key K, or any other data, is first passed into SHA256 and the resulting digest is then passed into RIPEMD-160. The book writes the formula A = RIPEMD160(SHA256(K)), where K is the public key and A is the resulting commitment, a 160-bit (20-byte) number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The name HASH160 is also that of the script operation OP_HASH160, which performs the same calculation inside a script.

paras.text: HASH160 is the name of the combination RIPEMD160(SHA256(K)), in which a public key K, or any other data, is first passed into SHA256 and the resulting digest is then passed into RIPEMD-160. The book writes the formula A = RIPEMD160(SHA256(K)), where K is the public key and A is the resulting commitment, a 160-bit (20-byte) number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The name HASH160 is also that of the script operation OP_HASH160, which performs the same calculation inside a script.

The combination gives Bitcoin a short, fixed-size reference to an object of any length. The same construction is used for both main legacy outputs: the commitment to a public key in a pay to public key hash output and the commitment to a script in a pay to script hash output, where the book says that it uses the same HASH160 mechanism, RIPEMD160(SHA256(script)) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

For the book's example private key the chapter's checks compute HASH160 of the compressed public key and obtain bbc1e42a39d05a4cc61752d6963b7f69d09bb27b, whose base58check form with version byte 0 is the address 1J7mdg5rbQyUHENYdx39WVWK7fsLpEoXZy. Hashing the uncompressed form of the same public key gives the different value 211b74ca4686f81efda5641767fc84ef16dafe0b and the different address 1424C2F4bC9JidNjjTUZCbUxv6Sa1Mt62x. The values match the output scripts that Bitcoin Core 31.1 reported when asked to validate the two addresses (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The calculation is mechanical. Take the bytes of the public key, compute SHA256, compute RIPEMD-160 of that digest, and keep the 20 bytes that result. In an output script the operation OP_HASH160 replaces the top item of the stack by its HASH160, so that the comparison with a stored commitment can be made by the script itself, as the sections on legacy scripts show (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

HASH160 commits to bytes, not to a mathematical point, so the same key written in two formats gives two different commitments. The book stresses that a single private key can produce a public key expressed in two formats, compressed and uncompressed, that produce two different addresses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The strength is that of a 160-bit function, no more, and the book recommends newer address types for this reason.

nodes.definition: HASH160 is the RIPEMD-160 of the SHA256 of the data; for the book's compressed example key it is bbc1e42a39d05a4cc61752d6963b7f69d09bb27b, and the uncompressed form of the same key gives a different value.

nodes.label: Format
nodes.body: This branch is about writing the same information down in different ways. A private key, a public key and a hash commitment are all numbers, and a number can be shown in binary, in hexadecimal, in a compact alphabet with a built-in checksum, or in a two-dimensional barcode. The choice of representation never changes the number, but it decides how long the text is, how easily a person can read it aloud, how likely a copying mistake is and whether the software can notice the mistake.

paras.text: This branch is about writing the same information down in different ways. A private key, a public key and a hash commitment are all numbers, and a number can be shown in binary, in hexadecimal, in a compact alphabet with a built-in checksum, or in a two-dimensional barcode. The choice of representation never changes the number, but it decides how long the text is, how easily a person can read it aloud, how likely a copying mistake is and whether the software can notice the mistake.

Representation matters in Bitcoin because mistakes are expensive. The book points out that any mistake made in copying a commitment would result in the bitcoins being sent to an unspendable output, causing them to be lost forever (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A payment cannot be recalled by a bank, so the text that Alice copies from Bob must either be correct or be recognised as incorrect before the money moves. All the formats of this branch are answers to that single concern, and the checksums in particular turn silent errors into visible ones.

The formats appear in every wallet. Hexadecimal and raw binary are used internally in software and rarely shown to users, while the wallet import format is used for importing and exporting keys between wallets and for printing them as barcodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Addresses use the base58check or the bech32 family of encodings, and the first character or the first few characters of such a string tell a trained eye which kind of data it is.

The branch has three levels of content. The first covers the basic ways to count and store data, bits, bytes, number bases and barcodes. The second covers the encodings of keys: the compressed and the uncompressed public key, the wallet import format of a private key, and the oddly named compressed private key. The third covers checksummed text: the checksum, the base58check procedure built from it, the version prefix that identifies the data type and the choice between the main network and the test network.

Never judge two strings to be different data merely because they look different, and never judge them equal merely because they begin alike. The book's central example is a single private key that appears in three different formats and a single public key that appears in two formats and yields two different addresses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Keeping the data and its representation apart in the mind is the central discipline of this branch.

nodes.label: Representation of data
nodes.body: The representation of data is the way a value is written down: as a count of bits, as a sequence of bytes, as digits in some number base, or as a picture that a camera can read. One and the same number has all of these forms at once, and none of them is more real than the others. This level gathers the three basic notions on which the encodings of the rest of the chapter build, so that a later section can speak of 65 bytes, of 130 hexadecimal digits or of a scanned code without having to explain itself again.

paras.text: The representation of data is the way a value is written down: as a count of bits, as a sequence of bytes, as digits in some number base, or as a picture that a camera can read. One and the same number has all of these forms at once, and none of them is more real than the others. This level gathers the three basic notions on which the encodings of the rest of the chapter build, so that a later section can speak of 65 bytes, of 130 hexadecimal digits or of a scanned code without having to explain itself again.

Every length that the chapter quotes, 32 bytes, 65 bytes, 130 hexadecimal digits, is a statement about a representation, and every conversion between formats is a change of representation. A reader who is not at ease with bits, bytes and number bases will find the later sections impossible to follow, so they are defined here before they are used.

A representation works by fixing two things: an alphabet of symbols, and a rule for reading a sequence of them as a number. The number is what exists; the text is one of many ways of writing it. Choosing a larger alphabet makes the text shorter, because each symbol carries more of the number - a byte written in base sixteen takes two characters, in base fifty-eight roughly one and a third, in base thirty-two exactly one and three fifths - and choosing which symbols the alphabet leaves out decides how safely a person can copy the text by hand. That is why the formats of this chapter differ: one drops the characters that look alike, another uses one case only so the text can be spoken and packed into a barcode. A picture such as a barcode is the same choice taken further, with the alphabet made of marks rather than letters (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

The reader meets these three notions in every length the chapter quotes. A private key is thirty-two bytes, which is sixty-four hexadecimal digits and fifty-one characters in the wallet's export format; an uncompressed public key is sixty-five bytes and a hundred and thirty hexadecimal digits; a native-segwit address of this chapter is forty-two characters of a thirty-two symbol alphabet. Each of those statements is about a representation and not about a different value, and the chapter's own figures for them are computed rather than quoted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that a conversion can lose information even when it looks harmless. Case is the common trap: the older format distinguishes upper from lower case and the newer one does not, so a reader who writes an older address in capitals has destroyed it, while writing a newer one in capitals is permitted and changes nothing. The second trap is the leading zero: a number has no leading zeros but a byte string does, and an encoding that forgets them produces text of the wrong length, which is why the procedure later in this chapter handles them as a separate step (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Bits and bytes
nodes.body: A bit is a binary digit, which has the value 0 or 1, and a byte is a group of 8 bits. Sizes in Bitcoin are quoted in both units, and the chapter moves between them freely: the book describes a private key as 256 bits shown as 64 hexadecimal digits of 4 bits each (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), a hash commitment as 160 bits or 20 bytes, and a public key as 65 bytes or 33 bytes.

paras.text: A bit is a binary digit, which has the value 0 or 1, and a byte is a group of 8 bits. Sizes in Bitcoin are quoted in both units, and the chapter moves between them freely: the book describes a private key as 256 bits shown as 64 hexadecimal digits of 4 bits each (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), a hash commitment as 160 bits or 20 bytes, and a public key as 65 bytes or 33 bytes.

The units decide how much space data takes and how large the space of possible values is. A value of 256 bits can take 2 to the 256 different values, which is the reason for the book's statement that the private key space is unfathomably large (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), while a value of 20 bytes has 160 bits and therefore only 2 to the 160 possible values. When the chapter later compares the strength of different commitments, it is comparing numbers of bits.

Everywhere in the chapter you will find the conversion between the two units. The book gives the uncompressed public key as a 520-bit number of 130 hexadecimal digits, and the compressed one as a number of 264 bits in 66 hexadecimal digits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). These are the same lengths as 65 and 33 bytes, because 65 times 8 is 520 and 33 times 8 is 264, and because a hexadecimal digit carries 4 bits, so two digits make one byte; the chapter's checks verify these equalities.

In Python a sequence of bytes is the type bytes, bytes.fromhex turns a string of hexadecimal digits into bytes, and the method hex() turns bytes back into digits. The built-in function len returns the number of bytes, and an integer has a bit_length() method. These few tools are all that the chapter's examples need to move between a key as a number, as bytes and as text.

The most frequent mistake is to mix up the number of digits with the number of bytes: 64 hexadecimal digits are 32 bytes, not 64. Another is to forget that a byte is an unsigned quantity, so that the byte 0x80 stands for 128 and not for a negative number. Count carefully and state the unit.

nodes.definition: A bit is a binary digit, 0 or 1; a byte is 8 bits; a public key of 65 bytes has 520 bits, and each hexadecimal digit stands for 4 bits.

nodes.label: Number base (hexadecimal, base58, base64)
nodes.body: A number base, also called a radix, is the number of distinct symbols that a notation uses for writing numbers. The traditional decimal system uses 10 numerals, 0 through 9, and the hexadecimal system uses 16, with the letters A through F as the six additional symbols. The book adds that a number written in hexadecimal is shorter than the equivalent decimal representation, and that base64 representation uses 26 lowercase letters, 26 capital letters, 10 numerals and 2 more characters such as + and /, in order to transmit binary data over text-based media such as email (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A number base, also called a radix, is the number of distinct symbols that a notation uses for writing numbers. The traditional decimal system uses 10 numerals, 0 through 9, and the hexadecimal system uses 16, with the letters A through F as the six additional symbols. The book adds that a number written in hexadecimal is shorter than the equivalent decimal representation, and that base64 representation uses 26 lowercase letters, 26 capital letters, 10 numerals and 2 more characters such as + and /, in order to transmit binary data over text-based media such as email (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The bigger the alphabet, the fewer symbols are needed for the same number, which is why compact formats are attractive for things that people have to copy. The book introduces base58 for this reason: it is a similar encoding to base64 that uses upper- and lowercase letters and numbers, but omits some characters that are frequently mistaken for one another and can appear identical when displayed in certain fonts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A larger alphabet gains length, a careful alphabet gains reliability, and base58 is a compromise.

Hexadecimal is the notation in which the chapter prints keys, hashes and coordinates, and base58 is the notation of legacy addresses and of keys in the wallet import format. Base64 is mentioned by the book only for comparison. Bech32, which later sections introduce, is a base 32 notation. The chapter's checks confirm that the base58 alphabet has 58 distinct characters, that it is the base64 alphabet without the six characters 0, O, l, I, + and /, and that the same private key needs fewer symbols in each larger base.

Writing a number in base b means finding its digits when it is divided repeatedly by b. In Python int(text, 16) reads hexadecimal and int(text, 2) reads binary, so that ff and 11111111 both give 255. For base58 the book gives the alphabet 123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz, whose symbols stand for the values 0 to 57 in order (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); a number is divided by 58 again and again, and each remainder selects one symbol. The one-expression example of the wallet import format in a later concept does exactly that.

A symbol means different things in different bases, and an alphabet is meaningful only together with its order. The digit 1 is the value one in decimal and hexadecimal but is the first symbol, the value 0, in the base58 alphabet, a fact that explains why leading zero bytes appear as the character 1 in addresses. Base conversion also needs care with leading zeros, which a number does not have but a byte string does.

nodes.definition: A number base, or radix, is the count of different symbols used to write numbers; hexadecimal uses 16, base64 uses 64 and base58 uses 58, and the same number is shorter in a larger base.

nodes.label: QR code
nodes.body: A QR code is a two-dimensional barcode, a square pattern of dots, that a phone camera can read to obtain a short piece of text such as an address or an invoice. Wallets use it because it removes typing altogether: the book notes that QR codes are commonly used to share addresses and invoices between wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 2 already showed a QR code that carried a payment request with an address, an amount and a label.

paras.text: A QR code is a two-dimensional barcode, a square pattern of dots, that a phone camera can read to obtain a short piece of text such as an address or an invoice. Wallets use it because it removes typing altogether: the book notes that QR codes are commonly used to share addresses and invoices between wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 2 already showed a QR code that carried a payment request with an address, an amount and a label.

The size of the text decides the size of the picture. The book observes that a mixed-case alphabet requires extra space in QR codes, so that the codes need to be larger at the same resolution or become harder to scan quickly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The proposal that introduced bech32 lists the same point among its motivations: base58 needs a lot of space in QR codes, as it cannot use the alphanumeric mode (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). A smaller picture scans faster and is more tolerant of poor cameras.

QR codes are met next to cash registers, on invoices, on paper wallets and on screens. The proposal for pay to script hash named them as a reason for short commitments, saying that a 20-byte hash is short enough to scan from a QR code or easily copied and pasted (Andresen, 2012). The book's figure of the same bech32 address encoded twice shows the effect in practice: the lowercase version and the uppercase version give two QR codes of visibly different size and complexity (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The bech32 specification says that encoders must always output a lowercase string, and that an uppercase version may be produced outside the encoding process, for presentation or for QR code use; decoders must not accept strings that mix uppercase and lowercase letters (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). Inside QR codes uppercase should be used, because uppercase permits the alphanumeric mode, which the proposal describes as 45 percent more compact than the normal byte mode (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). The chapter's checks confirm that the uppercase form of the book's address decodes to the same witness program as the lowercase form, and that a mixed-case form is rejected.

The saving applies only to alphabets that fit the alphanumeric mode, which is why base58 text, with its mixed case, cannot profit from it. Another caution is that the picture is only the address in a different form: whatever the camera reads is still text, and a careful wallet shows the decoded text so that the person can compare it with what was intended.

nodes.definition: A QR code is a two-dimensional barcode that a camera can read; its alphanumeric mode makes uppercase text about 45 percent more compact than the normal byte mode, which is why bech32 addresses are put into QR codes in uppercase.

nodes.label: Key encoding
nodes.body: A key encoding is a particular way of writing a key down as bytes or as text. The same private key has several (hexadecimal, wallet import format, wallet import format with a compression flag), and the same public key has two (compressed and uncompressed). All of them stand for the same underlying number or point, and the book stresses that any one format can easily be converted to any other (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A key encoding is a particular way of writing a key down as bytes or as text. The same private key has several (hexadecimal, wallet import format, wallet import format with a compression flag), and the same public key has two (compressed and uncompressed). All of them stand for the same underlying number or point, and the book stresses that any one format can easily be converted to any other (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Software that exports or imports keys must agree on the encoding, otherwise the receiving wallet may look for the wrong addresses. The book explains the case concretely: a wallet that imports keys from an older wallet needs to know whether to scan the blockchain for 65-byte keys and the commitments to them, or for 33-byte keys and their commitments, and failure to scan for the right type can lead to the user not being able to spend the full balance (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The encodings work by wrapping the same value in a few bytes that say how to read it. A public key is a point with two coordinates; writing both gives sixty-five bytes, but the curve's equation determines the second coordinate up to its sign, so a single byte recording which sign applies is enough and the compressed form is thirty-three bytes. The export form of a private key is the thirty-two secret bytes with a version byte in front, a checksum behind and, when the key belongs to a compressed public key, one extra byte in the middle whose only job is to tell the importing wallet which of the two public keys to derive. Nothing is encrypted and nothing is compressed in the ordinary sense: every one of these forms can be converted into any other, which is what the book means when it says the formats are interchangeable (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets the encodings whenever a key crosses a boundary between programs. A key handed to a learner in a tutorial is in hexadecimal; a key exported by a wallet for a backup is in the text format that begins with a recognisable character; a key inside a transaction is the compressed binary form. The place where the distinction bites is an import, because the receiving wallet has to decide which addresses to look for, and the chapter quotes the book's warning about exactly that case (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that one of these names is a misnomer and the book says so. Nothing about a private key is compressed; what the extra byte records is that the public key derived from it should be the compressed one. A learner who reads the name literally will expect the key itself to be shorter, find that it is not, and distrust the rest of the section. The second caution is that these text forms carry the secret in plain sight: an exported private key is the funds, and the chapter's section on passphrase protection exists because a backup of one is as sensitive as the wallet it came from (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Compressed public key
nodes.body: A compressed public key is an encoding of a public key that stores the x coordinate and one extra byte instead of both coordinates. When Bitcoin was first written its developers only knew how to create 65-byte public keys; a later developer found an alternative encoding that used only 33 bytes and was backward compatible with all Bitcoin full nodes at the time, so that the protocol did not need to change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The 33-byte keys are called compressed public keys and the original 65-byte keys are called uncompressed public keys.

paras.text: A compressed public key is an encoding of a public key that stores the x coordinate and one extra byte instead of both coordinates. When Bitcoin was first written its developers only knew how to create 65-byte public keys; a later developer found an alternative encoding that used only 33 bytes and was backward compatible with all Bitcoin full nodes at the time, so that the protocol did not need to change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The 33-byte keys are called compressed public keys and the original 65-byte keys are called uncompressed public keys.

Smaller keys make smaller transactions, and smaller transactions let more payments fit into the same block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Omitting the 256-bit y coordinate reduces the size of the key by almost 50 percent, which the chapter's checks put at 49.2 percent, and the saving is repeated in every transaction that reveals a key. Compressed public keys are now the default in almost all Bitcoin software and were required for certain features added by later protocol upgrades (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The compressed form of the book's example key is 03F028892BAD7ED57D2FB57BF33081D5CFCF6F9ED3D3D7F159C2E2FFF579DC341A, a number of 264 bits written in 66 hexadecimal digits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is the form that modern wallets hash into addresses, and it is the form that the 'compressed' private key format of a later concept announces. Older wallets that still use the uncompressed form are the reason why software must be able to read both.

The method rests on the curve equation. Since the point (x, y) satisfies y squared = x cubed + 7, knowing x leaves only two possible values of y, which are a number and its negative modulo p, the mirror pair of the curve's symmetry (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). One of the two is even and the other is odd, because p is odd, so a single prefix byte settles the choice: 02 means that y is even and 03 means that y is odd (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For the book's key the y coordinate ends in B, an odd digit, hence the prefix 03. The chapter's checks recover the full point from the 33 bytes by computing a modular square root, and they find the original coordinates.

Compression changes the bytes that are hashed. The same private key gives two public key formats, and if the compressed key is turned into a commitment with HASH160 it produces a different commitment from the uncompressed key, leading to a different address; the private key is identical for both addresses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet that scans for only one of the two forms will miss funds that were paid to the other.

nodes.definition: A compressed public key keeps only x and one byte for the parity of y, 33 bytes instead of 65, and the y coordinate is recovered by solving the curve equation.

nodes.label: Uncompressed public key
nodes.body: An uncompressed public key is the original encoding of a public key: the prefix byte 04 followed by the 32-byte x coordinate and the 32-byte y coordinate, 65 bytes in all. The book writes it as 04 x y and shows the example key as a 520-bit number of 130 hexadecimal digits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The shortest version of Bitcoin public keys known to the early developers was this 65-byte form, the equivalent of 130 characters in hexadecimal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An uncompressed public key is the original encoding of a public key: the prefix byte 04 followed by the 32-byte x coordinate and the 32-byte y coordinate, 65 bytes in all. The book writes it as 04 x y and shows the example key as a 520-bit number of 130 hexadecimal digits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The shortest version of Bitcoin public keys known to the early developers was this 65-byte form, the equivalent of 130 characters in hexadecimal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Understanding the uncompressed form is necessary because it has not disappeared. The book says that some software still needs to support uncompressed public keys, such as a wallet application importing private keys from an older wallet, and that such a wallet must scan for both kinds of key and for commitments to both (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The funds paid to an address built from an uncompressed key can only be spent by presenting that same uncompressed key.

Early Bitcoin addresses, some of which still hold funds, were built from uncompressed keys. The book's example key gives the P2PKH address 1424C2F4bC9JidNjjTUZCbUxv6Sa1Mt62x in this form, and Bitcoin Core 31.1 returned the same address when asked for the address of that uncompressed key and called it valid (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This is a different address from the one derived from the compressed form of the same key.

The prefix byte 04 tells the reader that both coordinates follow. To obtain the uncompressed form from a compressed one, software performs the square-root calculation described in the previous concept, and to compress, it keeps x and the parity of y. The two conversions lose nothing in either direction, which the chapter's checks demonstrate by a round trip on the example key.

Since the compressed and uncompressed keys are two encodings of one point, they are easily taken for two different keys. They correspond to the same private key, yet they lead to different HASH160 values and different legacy addresses, and a user who exports a key from an old wallet without recording which form it used may later look in the wrong place for the balance.

nodes.definition: An uncompressed public key is the prefix 04 followed by the x and y coordinates, 65 bytes, and it hashes to a different address than the compressed form of the same key.

nodes.label: Wallet import format (WIF)
nodes.body: The wallet import format, abbreviated WIF, is the text form in which a private key is exported from one wallet and imported into another. It is the base58check encoding of the version byte 0x80 followed by the 32-byte private key, and, for keys that produce compressed public keys, an extra byte 01 at the end (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For the book's example key the WIF is 5J3mBbAH58CpQ3Y5RNJpUKPE62SQ5tfcvU2JpbnkeyhfsYB1Jcn, and the compressed WIF is KxFC1jmwwCoACiCAWZ3eXa96mBM6tb3TYzGmf6YwgdGWZgawvrtJ.

paras.text: The wallet import format, abbreviated WIF, is the text form in which a private key is exported from one wallet and imported into another. It is the base58check encoding of the version byte 0x80 followed by the 32-byte private key, and, for keys that produce compressed public keys, an extra byte 01 at the end (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For the book's example key the WIF is 5J3mBbAH58CpQ3Y5RNJpUKPE62SQ5tfcvU2JpbnkeyhfsYB1Jcn, and the compressed WIF is KxFC1jmwwCoACiCAWZ3eXa96mBM6tb3TYzGmf6YwgdGWZgawvrtJ.

A raw 64-digit hexadecimal number is awkward to copy and carries no protection against typing errors. The WIF gives the key a recognisable first character and a checksum, so that a wallet can reject a mistyped key instead of importing a different one. The book says that the WIF is used for import and export of keys between wallets and often for QR code representations of private keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The WIF is met when someone moves a single key from an old wallet to a new one, and in older instructions for paper wallets and key backups. The book notes, however, that modern wallets generate all their keys from a single seed and rarely allow a single key to be imported or exported, so that the information about private key formats is mainly of interest to anyone needing compatibility with early Bitcoin wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A later concept on key export describes what Bitcoin Core did about the question.

The procedure has four steps. Put the version byte 0x80 in front of the key, add the byte 01 behind it if the key is for compressed public keys, append the first four bytes of the double SHA256 of the result, and write the whole in the base58 alphabet. The chapter's checks do this in one expression and obtain the book's WIF string, and with the extra byte they obtain the book's compressed string. Decoding reverses the steps and verifies the four checksum bytes. Without the suffix the result is 51 characters long and with it 52, and the first character is always 5 for the first and K or L for the second.

A WIF string is a private key, to be treated like one: anyone who sees it can spend the funds. Do not paste it into web pages, do not photograph it and do not mix up the two forms. The first character is the safety signal: 5 means that the wallet must look for the uncompressed public key and its addresses, and K or L means that it must look for the compressed ones (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: The wallet import format is the base58check encoding of version byte 0x80 and the private key, with a 0x01 suffix for the compressed form, which changes the first character from 5 to K or L.

nodes.label: Compressed private key
nodes.body: The commonly used term 'compressed private key' is a misnomer. When a private key is exported as WIF-compressed it is actually one byte longer than an 'uncompressed' private key, because it has an added one-byte suffix, shown as 01 in hexadecimal, which signifies that the private key is from a newer wallet and should only be used to produce compressed public keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Private keys are not themselves compressed and cannot be compressed.

paras.text: The commonly used term 'compressed private key' is a misnomer. When a private key is exported as WIF-compressed it is actually one byte longer than an 'uncompressed' private key, because it has an added one-byte suffix, shown as 01 in hexadecimal, which signifies that the private key is from a newer wallet and should only be used to produce compressed public keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Private keys are not themselves compressed and cannot be compressed.

The distinction prevents a practical error. The term really means 'private key from which only compressed public keys should be derived', and the term 'uncompressed private key' really means 'private key from which only uncompressed public keys should be derived' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book therefore advises referring to the export format as WIF-compressed or WIF and not to the private key itself as compressed, to avoid further confusion.

The flag shows up in exported keys. The hexadecimal form of the book's example with the suffix is the original 64 digits followed by 01, and the base58check form begins with K or L. The base58 version prefix is the same, 0x80, for both WIF and WIF-compressed; the extra byte changes the length of the number and therefore the first character from 5 to K or L (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book offers an analogy: the difference is like that between the decimal numbers 100 and 99, where 100 is one digit longer and also has a prefix of 1 instead of 9. As the length changes, it affects the prefix, and in base58 the prefix 5 changes to K or L as the length increases by one byte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's checks confirm the mechanism for the extreme keys, the smallest and the largest possible 32-byte values: without the suffix the first character is 5, with it the first character is K or L, and the decoded payload has 34 bytes against 33 bytes without the suffix when the version byte is counted.

The formats are not used interchangeably. In a newer wallet that implements compressed public keys the private keys are only ever exported as WIF-compressed with a K or L prefix, and in an older implementation that does not use compressed public keys they are exported as WIF with a prefix of 5 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The goal is to signal to the importing wallet whether it must search the blockchain for compressed or uncompressed public keys and addresses. Treat the suffix as a message, not as a compression.

nodes.definition: A 'compressed private key' is not compressed: it is the private key followed by a one-byte suffix 01 that says only compressed public keys should be derived from it, so its WIF is one character longer.

nodes.label: Checksummed text
nodes.body: Checksummed text is text that carries a few extra characters computed from the rest, so that the reader of the text can detect a copying mistake. Base58check is the first such format in this chapter and bech32 is the second. This level gathers the notion of the checksum, the base58check procedure, the version prefix that is part of the data it protects, and the distinction between networks that the prefix expresses.

paras.text: Checksummed text is text that carries a few extra characters computed from the rest, so that the reader of the text can detect a copying mistake. Base58check is the first such format in this chapter and bech32 is the second. This level gathers the notion of the checksum, the base58check procedure, the version prefix that is part of the data it protects, and the distinction between networks that the prefix expresses.

An address is typed, read aloud or copied by people, and a payment to a mistyped address is lost. A checksum is the cheapest defence: the wallet recomputes the check and refuses an address that does not match. The book states the benefit in a single sentence, that the check prevents a mistyped Bitcoin address from being accepted by the wallet software as a valid destination, an error that would otherwise result in loss of funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A checksum works by adding characters that are a function of everything before them, so that the valid strings are a tiny scattered subset of all the strings that could be written. The older format of this chapter hashes the version byte together with the payload, twice, and appends the first four bytes of the result; a decoder recomputes the hash and compares. Because the four bytes are thirty-two bits, a string altered at random passes by chance about once in four thousand million attempts, and because a hash spreads any change over the whole output, there is no family of mistakes it is systematically blind to. What such a check cannot do is say where the mistake was or repair it - it only refuses - and the newer format of the next level was designed with that limitation in mind. The version byte sits inside the protected data rather than beside it, which is why altering the byte that decides the network also breaks the check (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

The reader meets the check as the wallet's refusal. Pasting an address with one character changed produces an error rather than a payment, and that error is this section at work; the same check runs on an imported private key and on an extended key of chapter 5. The reader meets the version byte as the first character of the text, which is why an address beginning with one digit and an address beginning with another are recognisably different kinds, and why a key or an address for the test network cannot be mistaken for one on the main network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is about what the guarantee covers. The check catches mistakes in copying; it cannot catch an address that was copied perfectly from the wrong place. A string substituted by malicious software, or taken from the wrong line of a message, is a valid address with a valid checksum and the payment is final. The second caution is that four bytes is a defence against accident and not against a determined search, which is the difference between a checksum and the cryptographic commitments elsewhere in this chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Checksum
nodes.body: A checksum is a short value derived from a piece of data and attached to it. Anyone who has the data and the attached value can recompute the check and see whether they still agree; if the data was altered, they will with overwhelming probability disagree. In base58check the checksum is an additional four bytes added to the end of the data being encoded, derived from the hash of that data, and therefore able to detect transcription and typing errors (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A checksum is a short value derived from a piece of data and attached to it. Anyone who has the data and the attached value can recompute the check and see whether they still agree; if the data was altered, they will with overwhelming probability disagree. In base58check the checksum is an additional four bytes added to the end of the data being encoded, derived from the hash of that data, and therefore able to detect transcription and typing errors (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Detection is worth a lot even without correction. When the decoding software calculates the checksum of the data and compares it with the one included in the code, a mismatch means that an error has been introduced and the data is invalid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The wallet can then ask for the address again. The only alternative is to send the money and find out afterwards.

Checksums are common outside Bitcoin, in the check digits of identification numbers and in file downloads. Inside the chapter they appear twice: as the four bytes of base58check, and as the six characters of a bech32 address, which the book describes as a checksum produced by a BCH code that is exactly 6 characters long (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In both cases the checksum carries no information of its own.

The check is only as strong as its length. Four bytes are 32 bits, so a string that was changed at random still passes the base58check test with probability 1 in 2 to the 32, about 2.3 times 10 to the minus 10, and six bech32 characters are 30 bits, giving less than 1 in 10 to the 9, which is the figure the bech32 proposal states for errors beyond the guaranteed ones (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). The chapter's checks recompute the four checksum bytes of the book's P2PKH address from its first 21 bytes and find them equal to the last four, and they show that changing one character of the address breaks the check.

A checksum detects accident, not attack. Anyone who changes an address on purpose can compute a new valid checksum, so the check protects against typing mistakes and not against a malicious replacement of the whole string. It also says nothing about whether the address is the one you meant: a perfectly valid address that belongs to someone else passes every check.

nodes.definition: A checksum is a short value computed from data and attached to it so that a changed copy can be detected; base58check uses the first four bytes of a double SHA256, a mistyped address fails the check.

nodes.label: Base58check encoding
nodes.body: Base58check is the encoding that Bitcoin's legacy addresses and exported private keys use. It combines three ingredients: a version byte in front of the data, a checksum of four bytes behind it, and the base58 alphabet, which consists of lowercase and capital letters and numbers without the four characters 0, O, l and I (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's alphabet is 123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz, with 58 symbols.

paras.text: Base58check is the encoding that Bitcoin's legacy addresses and exported private keys use. It combines three ingredients: a version byte in front of the data, a checksum of four bytes behind it, and the base58 alphabet, which consists of lowercase and capital letters and numbers without the four characters 0, O, l and I (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's alphabet is 123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz, with 58 symbols.

The design serves people. Omitting the characters that look alike in certain fonts reduces misreading, the version prefix makes the type of data visible at a glance, and the checksum lets software refuse a damaged string. The book explains that this prevents a mistyped Bitcoin address from being accepted by the wallet software as a valid destination (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A shorter representation also takes less room on paper and in messages than a hexadecimal one.

Base58check is used in the legacy P2PKH and P2SH addresses and in the wallet import format of private keys, and, as the book says, other data besides public key commitments are presented in it to make that data compact, easy to read and easy to check (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's table of version prefixes lists addresses, private keys and the extended public key among the data types that use it.

To encode, first add the version byte to the data. Then compute the checksum as the SHA256 of the SHA256 of the prefix followed by the data, the book's double-SHA checksum, and keep the first four bytes of the resulting 32-byte hash. Append the four bytes, and write the three-part result as a number in base58 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's checks do this for the book's key: the double SHA256 of the version byte and the key begins with the four bytes that the WIF string ends with when decoded, and the toolkit's decoder verifies them again. A leading version byte of zero becomes the character 1 in front of the text.

Base58check is not secure encoding, and it is not even particularly efficient to compute. The bech32 proposal lists its limitations as a double SHA256 checksum that is slow and has no error-detection guarantees, a mixed case that is inconvenient to read aloud and to place in a QR code, and a decoding procedure that is complicated and relatively slow, and these are reasons why newer address types moved to another format (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). The book names the same weaknesses, adding that the format can detect errors but cannot help correct them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Version prefix
nodes.body: The version prefix, which the book calls the version byte, is the first byte of the data that base58check encodes, and it identifies the type of data. The prefix zero, 0x00 in hexadecimal, indicates that the data is the commitment of a legacy pay to public key hash output script; the book's table lists 0x00 for a P2PKH address, 0x05 for a P2SH address, 0x6F and 0xC4 for the testnet counterparts, 0x80 for a private key in WIF and 0x0488B21E for a BIP32 extended public key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The version prefix, which the book calls the version byte, is the first byte of the data that base58check encodes, and it identifies the type of data. The prefix zero, 0x00 in hexadecimal, indicates that the data is the commitment of a legacy pay to public key hash output script; the book's table lists 0x00 for a P2PKH address, 0x05 for a P2SH address, 0x6F and 0xC4 for the testnet counterparts, 0x80 for a private key in WIF and 0x0488B21E for a BIP32 extended public key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The prefix makes data self-describing. Because the version byte is encoded together with the rest, each prefix gives encoded strings that begin with specific characters, which makes it easy for humans to identify the type of data and how to use it. This is what differentiates, for example, a base58check-encoded address that starts with 1 from a private key in WIF that starts with 5 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The resulting leading characters are the ones people recognise: 1 for P2PKH addresses, 3 for P2SH addresses, m or n for testnet P2PKH addresses, 2 for testnet P2SH addresses, 5, K or L for private keys in WIF and the letters xpub for extended public keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The extended public key belongs to the wallet structures that Chapter 5 will present. The chapter's checks encode data of each prefix and show the first characters that come out.

The leading character is a consequence of the numbers and not an extra field: the prefix byte is the most significant part of a number that is then written in base 58, so its value selects the first digit or the first few. For a 20-byte payload the version 0x00 gives the character 1, the version 0x05 gives 3, and the version 0xC4 gives 2; 0x6F gives m or n depending on the payload, as the checks show for the smallest and the largest payloads. For a 32-byte payload the version 0x80 gives 5, and with the suffix 01 it gives K or L.

The prefix identifies the type; it does not authenticate the data. A string that starts with 1 and passes the checksum test is a plausible P2PKH address, nothing more: it may belong to anyone, and it may belong to a key that nobody holds any longer. Nor does the prefix tell the payer which script the receiver will use to spend, since the version byte names a template and the template is the same for every receiver. The prefixes of the book's table apply to base58check only; bech32 addresses express the same two ideas, the network and the kind of output, through the human-readable part and the witness version, as a later section explains.
