nodes.label: Segwit inside P2SH
nodes.body: Segwit inside P2SH, often called nested segwit, is the way in which a receiver can use segregated witness through an ordinary P2SH address. The redeem script that the address commits to is the segwit output script itself: the byte for version 0 followed by a push of the 20-byte hash of the public key. The book explains the idea: as the P2SH output type had the advantage that a spender does not need to know the details of the script the receiver uses, the segwit upgrade was designed to use that mechanism, allowing users to begin accessing many of its benefits immediately through a P2SH address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Segwit inside P2SH, often called nested segwit, is the way in which a receiver can use segregated witness through an ordinary P2SH address. The redeem script that the address commits to is the segwit output script itself: the byte for version 0 followed by a push of the 20-byte hash of the public key. The book explains the idea: as the P2SH output type had the advantage that a spender does not need to know the details of the script the receiver uses, the segwit upgrade was designed to use that mechanism, allowing users to begin accessing many of its benefits immediately through a P2SH address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Nested segwit was a bridge. A receiver wanting segwit did not have to wait for all payers to upgrade, because every wallet that could pay a P2SH address could pay this one. The book adds the limit of the bridge: to gain access to all the benefits, Bob would need Alice's wallet to pay him with a different type of script, and that would require Alice's wallet to upgrade to support the new scripts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The bech32 address was the way out of the dilemma.

The nested form is still visible in Bitcoin Core, whose address type options are legacy, p2sh-segwit, bech32 and bech32m (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The documentation of descriptors calls the corresponding output a P2SH-P2WPKH output and writes it sh(wpkh(KEY)) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Such an address begins with 3 like every P2SH address, so it cannot be told from a multisignature P2SH address by looking at it.

The chapter's checks build one. The compressed public key of the example gives the 20-byte hash bbc1e42a39d05a4cc61752d6963b7f69d09bb27b; the redeem script is the two bytes 00 and 14 followed by that hash; the P2SH address of this script is 3FyC6EYuxW22uj4CaEGjNCjxeg7gHyFeVv. Bitcoin Core 31.1 returns the same address for the descriptor sh(wpkh(KEY)) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The payer sees only a P2SH output and nothing of the witness.

Compared with a native segwit address, the nested one costs more space: the specification gives the figures for the nested form of P2WPKH, an output script one byte bigger and an input script 23 bytes bigger than those of the native form (Lombrozo et al., 2015). It is also more roundabout, and the book's reasoning for the bech32 format is that it should lead directly to the new scripts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The nested kind also carries the weaker 160-bit commitment of P2SH, a point discussed under the collision attack. It is a compatibility measure and should not be mistaken for a separate kind of key.

nodes.definition: A P2SH address can wrap a witness program: the redeem script is the witness output script (OP_0 and the 20-byte key hash), so an older payer that only knows P2SH can pay a segwit receiver.

nodes.label: Bech32 address
nodes.body: A bech32 address is a segwit address written in the bech32 format, which is a checksummed base 32 format. The book gives its pronunciation, a soft ch as in besh thirty-two, and explains the name: bech stands for BCH, the initials of the three individuals who discovered the cyclic code in 1959 and 1960 on which the checksum is based, and 32 for the number of characters of the alphabet, as the 58 in base58check (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The designers' own explanation of the name is shorter: Bech contains the characters BCH, the error detection algorithm used, and sounds a bit like base (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

paras.text: A bech32 address is a segwit address written in the bech32 format, which is a checksummed base 32 format. The book gives its pronunciation, a soft ch as in besh thirty-two, and explains the name: bech stands for BCH, the initials of the three individuals who discovered the cyclic code in 1959 and 1960 on which the checksum is based, and 32 for the number of characters of the alphabet, as the 58 in base58check (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The designers' own explanation of the name is shorter: Bech contains the characters BCH, the error detection algorithm used, and sounds a bit like base (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

The format answers the defects of base58check that the designers identified. It uses only numbers and a single case of letters, which makes it easier to read aloud and to copy; it can detect, and help to locate, errors; it can be written in capital letters, which takes less space in a QR code; and it has a mechanism that lets today's wallets pay outputs of future versions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book adds that despite its alphabet being almost half the size of the base58check alphabet, a bech32 address for P2WPKH is only slightly longer than the legacy address for an equivalent P2PKH script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book's example, for a P2WPKH output, is bc1q9d3xa5gg45q2j39m9y32xzvygcgay4rgc6aaee, 42 characters long, and the book shows further examples for the other output kinds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core 31.1 reports the address as valid, as a witness address of version 0 whose program is 2b626ed108ad00a944bb2922a309844611d25468 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Version 0 addresses are always 42 or 62 characters long, as the specification says (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

An address is built in three steps. The witness version and the witness program are rearranged from groups of 8 bits into groups of 5, each group is replaced by one of the 32 characters of the alphabet qpzry9x8gf2tvdw0s3jn54khce6mua7l, and the checksum, six more characters, is computed over the human-readable part and the data and appended (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). The chapter's checks do it with the toolkit, which reproduces the book's address from the 20 bytes of the program, and also with the reference implementation that the book itself uses; both give the same four addresses of the book. Decoding reverses the steps and fails if the checksum is wrong.

The format has a weakness that appeared only in practice, described in the concept on length extension. The alphabet omits the characters 1, b, i and o because they resemble others (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017), but the string is still easy to mistype in the middle of a long address. A last caution concerns case: a bech32 address must be written entirely in lowercase or entirely in uppercase, and a decoder must not accept a string that mixes the two (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

nodes.definition: A bech32 address is a human-readable part, the separator 1, a witness version, a witness program and a six-character checksum, in one case of a 32-character alphabet.

nodes.label: Witness version
nodes.body: The witness version is a number between 0 and 16 that tells which set of rules governs a witness output. In a bech32m address it is a single byte that is encoded as a single character immediately following the separator. The book says that the letter q is the encoding of 0 for segwit version 0, the initial version, where bech32 addresses were introduced, and the letter p is the encoding of 1 for segwit version 1, also called taproot, where bech32m began to be used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). There are seventeen possible versions, and Bitcoin requires that the first byte of the data part decode to a number from 0 to 16 inclusive (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The witness version is a number between 0 and 16 that tells which set of rules governs a witness output. In a bech32m address it is a single byte that is encoded as a single character immediately following the separator. The book says that the letter q is the encoding of 0 for segwit version 0, the initial version, where bech32 addresses were introduced, and the letter p is the encoding of 1 for segwit version 1, also called taproot, where bech32m began to be used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). There are seventeen possible versions, and Bitcoin requires that the first byte of the data part decode to a number from 0 to 16 inclusive (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The version is the means by which the protocol can grow. A new kind of output receives a new version number, and wallets that can pay any version can pay it without a new address format. The designers' stated hope was that developers could build a wallet today that allows spending to a bech32 address and have that wallet remain able to pay bech32 addresses for users of new features added in future protocol upgrades (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That is why the book asks implementers to pass the test vectors concerning the versions that are not yet defined.

The characters follow from the alphabet: q is the character at position 0 and p at position 1, and the book's last example, an address for the highest version, begins with bc1s because s is at position 16 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's checks look the positions up in the alphabet of the specification. In the output script the version is stored as an opcode: version 0 is OP_0, which uses the byte 0x00, but version 1 uses OP_1, which is the byte 0x51, and the versions 2 to 16 use 0x52 to 0x60 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A decoder takes the first value after the separator, checks that it is between 0 and 16, and uses it to decide which checksum constant and which program lengths are allowed: for version 0 the bech32 constant and a program of 20 or 32 bytes, for versions 1 to 16 the bech32m constant (Wuille, 2020). The chapter's checks compute the opcode bytes from the versions, 0x00 for 0 and 0x50 plus the version for 1 to 16, and obtain the book's values 0x51 and 0x60 for the first and last of them, with the value 0x60 matching the opcode OP_16 in the source of Bitcoin Core (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book's warning is the most important thing to remember here: a witness version of 0 is OP_0, which uses the byte 0x00, but a witness version of 1 uses OP_1, the byte 0x51, and not 0x01 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet that converts an address to an output script with the wrong byte creates an output that is likely to be unspendable or insecure, as the specification warns (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). Another mistake is to think that the version is part of the program: it is a separate field.

nodes.definition: The witness version is the first character after the separator of a segwit address; it is a number from 0 to 16, and the character q stands for 0 and p for 1.

nodes.label: Witness program
nodes.body: The witness program is the data part of a segwit output: the bytes that follow the witness version in the output script and in the address. It is between 2 and 40 bytes long. For segwit version 0 it must be either 20 or 32 bytes, and no other length is valid; for version 1 the only length defined at the time of the book is 32 bytes, though others may be defined later (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The witness program is the data part of a segwit output: the bytes that follow the witness version in the output script and in the address. It is between 2 and 40 bytes long. For segwit version 0 it must be either 20 or 32 bytes, and no other length is valid; for version 1 the only length defined at the time of the book is 32 bytes, though others may be defined later (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The program is the commitment on which the receiver and the payer agree. In version 0 the 20-byte program commits to a public key and the 32-byte program to a script, which means that the decoder can tell what kind of output is meant from the length alone. The specification of the address format requires decoders to enforce the known-length restrictions for the versions that have them, and quotes BIP141: if the version byte is 0 but the witness program is neither 20 nor 32 bytes, the script must fail (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

The book's table shows the three kinds in use at the time of publication, together with a fourth for a future version: OP_0 and the 20-byte hash for P2WPKH, OP_0 and the 32-byte hash for P2WSH, OP_1 and the 32-byte point for P2TR, and OP_16 followed by two bytes of zero for a future example (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core reports the scripts for these addresses as 0014 and the program, 0020 and the program, 5120 and the program, and 60020000 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

From the length rules the address lengths follow. A program of 20 bytes gives an address of 42 characters, and one of 32 bytes gives an address of 62; the book says that these are the two lengths of version 0 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In general an address is between 14 and 74 characters long, and its length modulo 8 cannot be 0, 3 or 5, as the specification derives from the rules (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). The chapter's checks compute the lengths from the bit counts and the smallest and largest case.

The program is not the address, nor is it the script: it is only the data that a template wraps. The same bytes are a public key hash in one kind and the start of a script hash in another only by their length and version. A decoder that accepts a program of an invalid length for its version produces an address that cannot be spent.

nodes.definition: The witness program is 2 to 40 bytes and, for witness version 0, exactly 20 or 32; for version 1, taproot, it is a 32-byte point.

nodes.label: Human-readable part
nodes.body: The human-readable part, abbreviated HRP, is the beginning of a bech32 string: a short prefix of printable characters that conveys the type of data or anything else relevant to the reader. The book says that bech32m addresses start with it, and that for Bitcoin it needs to know only about the two already chosen: bc for Bitcoin mainnet and tb for Bitcoin testnet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The specification allows 1 to 83 characters in general and leaves applications to restrict them further (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

paras.text: The human-readable part, abbreviated HRP, is the beginning of a bech32 string: a short prefix of printable characters that conveys the type of data or anything else relevant to the reader. The book says that bech32m addresses start with it, and that for Bitcoin it needs to know only about the two already chosen: bc for Bitcoin mainnet and tb for Bitcoin testnet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The specification allows 1 to 83 characters in general and leaves applications to restrict them further (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

The prefix makes an address self-describing, and it keeps networks apart: an address written for one cannot be mistaken for the other, because the prefix is mixed into the checksum as well (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). The specification explains why the shorter bc was chosen and not btc: it is shorter; and tb has the same length as bc, which simplifies implementations' assumptions about lengths, yet is visually distinct (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

The human-readable part is followed by the separator, the number 1. The book explains the choice: earlier proposals used a colon, but some operating systems and applications that allow a user to double-click a word to highlight it for copy and paste do not extend the highlighting past a colon, whereas a number does work, and 1 was chosen because bech32 strings do not otherwise use it, which prevents accidental transliteration between the number 1 and the lowercase letter l (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The specification adds that if the prefix itself contains a 1, the last one in the string is the separator (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

To split an address, a decoder finds the last 1 in the string: everything before it is the prefix and everything after it is the data part, whose characters never include 1. The chapter's checks do so for the book's mainnet address and for the specification's testnet address for the same kind of output, and obtain bc and tb. In the checksum computation the high bits of each prefix character are processed first, then a zero, then the low bits, so that an error that changes a letter into another letter remains within the range for which the error-detection guarantee holds (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

Changing the prefix of a valid address does not give a valid address on the other network, because the checksum would no longer match; a tool that merely replaces bc by tb produces an invalid string. Nor should the prefix be confused with the version: the prefix names the network, while the character after the separator names the witness version.

nodes.example: bc for mainnet, tb for testnet
nodes.definition: The human-readable part opens a bech32 address and names its network or purpose, for Bitcoin bc for the main network and tb for testnet; it is followed by the separator 1.

nodes.label: BCH code
nodes.body: A BCH code is an error-correcting code, named after the initials of the discoverers of the cyclic code on which it is based, and it is the mathematical heart of the bech32 checksum. The book says that the checksum is exactly six characters long and is created using a BCH code, a type of error correction code, although for Bitcoin addresses it is essential to use the checksum only for error detection and not for correction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The specification of the format describes the code as implementing a BCH code that guarantees the detection of any error affecting at most four characters (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

paras.text: A BCH code is an error-correcting code, named after the initials of the discoverers of the cyclic code on which it is based, and it is the mathematical heart of the bech32 checksum. The book says that the checksum is exactly six characters long and is created using a BCH code, a type of error correction code, although for Bitcoin addresses it is essential to use the checksum only for error detection and not for correction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The specification of the format describes the code as implementing a BCH code that guarantees the detection of any error affecting at most four characters (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

The code gives bech32 a stronger guarantee than the checksum of base58check, which is only a truncated hash. A hash gives a probabilistic check; a BCH code can be designed so that a specific class of errors is detected with certainty. The specification states the proposition: any error affecting at most 4 characters is guaranteed to be detected, and there is less than a 1 in 10 to the 9 chance of failing to detect more errors (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

The six characters of a bech32 address carry 30 bits, since each character holds 5 bits, and 2 to the 30 is just over a billion, which is the origin of the one-in-a-billion figure for errors beyond the guarantee. The checksum contains no information of its own (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). The specification includes the code that checks it, a short function that computes a polynomial remainder over the numbers of the characters with five constants, and states that valid strings must pass it (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

The verification feeds the expanded prefix and the data characters through the function polymod, which combines each value into a running 30-bit state, and accepts the string if the final state equals a constant: 1 for bech32 and 0x2bc830a3 for bech32m (Wuille, 2020). The chapter's checks run the function on the book's address and accept it, then test the guarantee on that address. All 1,209 changes of one data character and all 712,101 changes of two data characters are detected, and so are all 100,000 random changes of three or four characters that the checks try.

Correction has a danger that detection does not. The specification warns that error correction erodes error detection, because correction changes invalid inputs into valid inputs, and if more than a few errors were made the valid input may not be the correct input; it therefore asks implementations not to correct beyond suggesting where in the string an error might be (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). Bitcoin Core follows the advice by pointing to the positions of the errors and nothing more (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: A BCH code is an error-correcting code; bech32's checksum is a BCH code of six 5-bit characters, 30 bits, which is why errors beyond the guaranteed ones slip through less than once in a billion.

nodes.label: Error detection
nodes.body: Error detection is the property of a format that lets software notice that a string has been altered by an accident, such as a mistyped character. The book states what bech32 gives: in an address of the expected length, it is mathematically guaranteed to detect any error affecting four characters or fewer, which is more reliable than base58check; for longer errors it fails to detect them less than one time in a billion, roughly the same reliability as base58check (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Beyond detection, for an address typed with just a few errors, it can tell the user where those errors occurred (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
