The book states what bech32 gives: in an address of the expected length, it is mathematically guaranteed to detect any error affecting four characters or fewer, which is more reliable than base58check; for longer errors it fails to detect them less than one time in a billion, roughly the same reliability as base58check (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Beyond detection, for an address typed with just a few errors, it can tell the user where those errors occurred (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A wallet that can say where the mistake is makes the correction quick. The book describes the experience with base58check: if you accidentally transpose two characters your wallet will almost certainly warn that a mistake exists but will not help you find it, and it might take several frustrating minutes to discover the mistake (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For bech32 the decoder can mark the positions of the characters in error, which turns a rejection into a repair.

The book shows an address with two errors, whose wrong characters are underlined in its figure. Bitcoin Core 31.1 rejects the address with the message Invalid Bech32m checksum and reports the error locations 25 and 40, and the chapter's checks confirm that these are exactly the two positions in which the typed string differs from the correct address (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book obtained its figure from a decoder demonstration that localises errors (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The mechanism rests on the BCH code: the checksum is a remainder that equals a fixed constant for valid strings, so a few wrong characters change the remainder. One of the properties of these BCH codes is that they can be used for error correction, which is what lets a decoder suggest where an error is (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). The guarantee holds only if the length of the string entered equals the length of the original address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's checks confirm the guarantee on the book's address by trying every single-character and every two-character substitution.

The guarantee has a condition that the book spells out: it applies only if the length of the address entered is the same as the length of the original. If characters are added or removed in transcription the guarantee does not apply and the wallet may spend funds to a wrong address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This is the root of the weakness explained in the next concept. Detection is also not correction: the specification asks software never to apply a suggested correction without the user's confirmation (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

nodes.definition: Bech32 is guaranteed to detect any error affecting four characters or fewer, and Bitcoin Core points to where a typing error is, while bech32's original constant let a q be added before a final p without detection, which bech32m fixes.

io.code: [i for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip('bc1p9nh05ha8wrljf7ru236awm4t2x0d5ctkkywmu9sclnm4t0av2vgs4k3au7', 'bc1p9nh05ha8wrljf7ru236awn4t2x0d5ctkkywmv9sclnm4t0av2vgs4k3au7')) if a != b]

nodes.label: Bech32 length extension weakness
nodes.body: The length extension weakness is a flaw found in the bech32 checksum after the format had been designed: the guarantees about detecting errors apply only if the length of the entered address is the same as that of the original. The book explains that one of the constants of the algorithm happened to make it very easy to add or remove the letter q in the penultimate position of an address that ends with the letter p, and to do so more than once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The specification of the repair says that whenever the final character is a p, inserting or deleting any number of q characters immediately preceding it does not invalidate the checksum (Wuille, 2020).

paras.text: The length extension weakness is a flaw found in the bech32 checksum after the format had been designed: the guarantees about detecting errors apply only if the length of the entered address is the same as that of the original. The book explains that one of the constants of the algorithm happened to make it very easy to add or remove the letter q in the penultimate position of an address that ends with the letter p, and to do so more than once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The specification of the repair says that whenever the final character is a p, inserting or deleting any number of q characters immediately preceding it does not invalidate the checksum (Wuille, 2020).

In version 0 the flaw is harmless in practice, because only two lengths of witness program are valid. The book works out the figures: the valid program lengths of 22 and 34 bytes of script correspond to addresses of 42 and 62 characters, so one would have to add or remove the letter q twenty times to send money to an invalid address without the wallet being able to detect it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For later versions it would become a problem, because developers did not want to constrain output sizes: without a constraint, adding or removing a single q could send money to an output that is unspendable or spendable by anyone (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book prints an intended address, bc1pqqqsq9txsqp, and five longer strings with a valid checksum. The chapter's checks verify the book's statement, by applying the checksum algorithm of bech32: all six strings carry a valid bech32 checksum, and none of them carries a valid bech32m checksum. Bitcoin Core 31.1 refuses all six when they are given as version 1 addresses (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The note in the specification of bech32m, that the flaw was reported in an issue of the repository of the reference implementation, shows how it was found (Wuille, 2020).

The lengths of the book's six strings show what has been inserted: the intended address has 15 characters and the five others have 18, 20, 22, 23 and 25, which means that three, five, seven, eight and ten letters q have been put in front of the final p. Because the string ends in that p, the checksum of bech32 stays valid after each of these insertions, and a decoder of that format cannot tell the six strings apart; the chapter's checks confirm the six lengths and that every one of the six passes the bech32 test. The repair, explained in the next concept, changes one constant of the algorithm and removes the flaw for insertions and deletions of up to five characters, as the book states (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The flaw does not affect segwit version 0 addresses or the funds that were sent to them, and it was fixed before it could harm users. The lesson for implementers is that a checksum has a design range, and that a property such as detecting any change of up to four characters says nothing about lengths. A further consequence is that wallets must reject addresses whose length is not valid for their version, which the specification's decoder does.

nodes.example: a q before a final p
nodes.definition: In bech32, adding or removing the letter q just before a final p leaves the checksum valid; the book's six extended strings are valid under bech32 and invalid under bech32m.

nodes.label: Bech32m address
nodes.body: Bech32m, short for bech32 modified, is the version of bech32 with a single different constant. The checksum algorithm is the same, and in its final step the constant 0x2bc830a3 is combined by an exclusive-or operation with the value in place of the constant 1 of the original (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2020). Bech32m is used for segwit outputs of version 1 and later, while version 0 keeps bech32 (Wuille, 2020). The book recommends it as the current address format for Bitcoin wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Bech32m, short for bech32 modified, is the version of bech32 with a single different constant. The checksum algorithm is the same, and in its final step the constant 0x2bc830a3 is combined by an exclusive-or operation with the value in place of the constant 1 of the original (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2020). Bech32m is used for segwit outputs of version 1 and later, while version 0 keeps bech32 (Wuille, 2020). The book recommends it as the current address format for Bitcoin wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The aim was to remove the length extension weakness without constraining future output sizes. The book reports that developers analysed the bech32 problem exhaustively and found that changing a single constant would eliminate it, so that any insertion or deletion of up to five characters is missed less often than one time in a billion (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The specification explains why version 0 was not given the choice of both encodings: permitting both would reduce the error detection capabilities, making it equivalent to having only 29 bits of checksum (Wuille, 2020).

All the characters of a bech32 and a bech32m address for the same underlying data are identical except for the last six, the checksum (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's taproot example, bc1p9nh05ha8wrljf7ru236awm4t2x0d5ctkkywmu9sclnm4t0av2vgs4k3au7, is a bech32m address, and Bitcoin Core 31.1 validates it as a witness address of version 1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A wallet needs to know which of the two versions is in use to validate the checksum, but the version inside the address makes that easy to find out (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

To decode, a program computes the polynomial remainder once and compares it with both constants: 1 means bech32, 0x2bc830a3 means bech32m, anything else is an error. It then checks that the encoding matches the witness version, bech32 for version 0 and bech32m for the others (Wuille, 2020). The chapter's checks encode the same 20-byte program once with each constant and find that the two strings share all characters except the last six, and the worked example shows the same for the book's taproot program, where the two encodings differ only in their last six characters, q2p3eu against 4k3au7. They also encode the program of the book's taproot address with the bech32 constant and see that a decoder that applies the rule rejects the result.

A bech32m address with a version 0 program is not valid, and a bech32 address with a version 1 program is not valid either; software that accepts both for either version loses part of the error detection. The BIP350 document states that a string can never be valid in both encodings, because two valid strings of equal length differ in at least three characters (Wuille, 2020). Implementers should use the test vectors of the specification, including those for versions that are not yet defined (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: Bech32m differs from bech32 only in the constant merged into the checksum, 0x2bc830a3 instead of 1, and is required for witness version 1 and later.

nodes.label: Pay to witness public key hash (P2WPKH)
nodes.body: Pay to witness public key hash, abbreviated P2WPKH, is the segwit counterpart of P2PKH. The output script is the witness version 0 followed by a 20-byte witness program, and for the book's example the script is OP_0 2b626ed108ad00a944bb2922a309844611d25468 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The witness program contains a commitment constructed in exactly the same way as the commitment for a P2PKH output: the public key is passed into SHA256, the 32-byte digest into RIPEMD-160, and the result is placed in the witness program (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Pay to witness public key hash, abbreviated P2WPKH, is the segwit counterpart of P2PKH. The output script is the witness version 0 followed by a 20-byte witness program, and for the book's example the script is OP_0 2b626ed108ad00a944bb2922a309844611d25468 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The witness program contains a commitment constructed in exactly the same way as the commitment for a P2PKH output: the public key is passed into SHA256, the 32-byte digest into RIPEMD-160, and the result is placed in the witness program (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The kind combines the short commitment of P2PKH with the benefits of the segwit upgrade, and it yields a bech32 address only slightly longer than the legacy one. Since the signature and the public key move into the witness, the transaction identifier no longer depends on them, which is the point of the upgrade (Lombrozo et al., 2015). A P2WPKH output is the form that Bitcoin Core hands out by default (Bitcoin Core, 2026), and the specification notes that it occupies 3 bytes less in the output script than the equivalent P2PKH output (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

For the book's example key the chapter's checks compute the program from the compressed public key, bbc1e42a39d05a4cc61752d6963b7f69d09bb27b, and obtain the address bc1qh0q7g23e6pdye3sh2ttfvwmld8gfhvnmmfxuck, the same as the descriptor wpkh(KEY) gives in Bitcoin Core 31.1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The specification of the address format shows the standard example: the public key of the generator point gives the program 751e76e8199196d454941c45d1b3a323f1433bd6 and the address bc1qw508d6qejxtdg4y5r3zarvary0c5xw7kv8f3t4 (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

The script is 22 bytes: one byte for the version 0, one for the length 20, and the 20 bytes of the commitment. A node that sees such an output recognises the pattern, and when the output is spent the spender supplies the signature and the public key in the witness, not in the input script; the witness must consist of exactly two items, a signature and a public key, and the HASH160 of the key must match the program (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The chapter's checks recompute the hash of the generator point's public key and confirm the specification's address.

The word hash in the name should not be read as an extra layer of secrecy: the commitment is only 160 bits and is subject to the collision attack of the legacy discussion, but for a key created by one party alone it is as strong as P2PKH. The kind carries one key only, and only compressed public keys are accepted in P2WPKH and P2WSH, so a key that was used in its uncompressed form with a legacy address cannot be used with this kind (Lombrozo et al., 2015); scripts with several keys need the next kind.

nodes.definition: A P2WPKH output script is OP_0 followed by the 20-byte HASH160 of a public key, the same commitment as P2PKH, 22 bytes in all; its address is bech32.

nodes.label: Pay to witness script hash (P2WSH)
nodes.body: Pay to witness script hash, abbreviated P2WSH, is the segwit counterpart of P2SH. The output script is the version 0 followed by a 32-byte witness program, which is the SHA256 digest of the script that will be revealed when the output is spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book stresses that the algorithm of P2SH is not used here: the script is passed into a SHA256 function and the 32-byte digest is used in the witness program, whereas P2SH hashed the SHA256 digest again with RIPEMD-160 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Pay to witness script hash, abbreviated P2WSH, is the segwit counterpart of P2SH. The output script is the version 0 followed by a 32-byte witness program, which is the SHA256 digest of the script that will be revealed when the output is spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book stresses that the algorithm of P2SH is not used here: the script is passed into a SHA256 function and the 32-byte digest is used in the witness program, whereas P2SH hashed the SHA256 digest again with RIPEMD-160 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The longer commitment is the answer to the collision attack. The book notes that for P2SH the RIPEMD-160 step may not be secure in some cases, as the collision discussion explains, and that a consequence of using SHA256 alone is that the commitments are 32 bytes (256 bits) instead of 20 bytes (160 bits) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The newer addresses thereby provide at least 128 bits of collision resistance, as the book says (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book's example is bc1qvj9r9egtd7mu2gemy28kpf4zefq4ssqzdzzycj7zjhk4arpavfhsct5a3p, 62 characters long, with the program 648a32e50b6fb7c5233b228f60a6a2ca4158400268844c4bc295ed5e8c3d626f. The specification of bech32 gives a worked example too: for the script formed of a public key and OP_CHECKSIG the SHA256 digest is 1863143c14c5166804bd19203356da136c985678cd4d27a1b8c6329604903262 (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). Bitcoin Core 31.1 validates the book's address as a witness address of version 0 and reports its script as a 34-byte one (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

To pay to a script the receiver computes the SHA256 of the serialised script and gives the digest to the payer in a bech32 address. To spend, the receiver provides the script in the witness, together with the data it needs, and nodes check that the script hashes to the program before running it (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The chapter's checks reproduce the specification's digest from its public key and the opcode OP_CHECKSIG, and the matching address.

The 32-byte program tells the node that it must be a script hash, but the script itself is not visible until the output is spent. As with P2SH, the payer cannot verify that the script can be satisfied. The stronger commitment protects against an attacker who helps to create the script, but it does not make a poorly designed script safe.

nodes.definition: A P2WSH output script is OP_0 followed by the 32-byte SHA256 of a script, without the RIPEMD-160 step of P2SH, 34 bytes in all.

nodes.label: Pay to taproot (P2TR)
nodes.body: Pay to taproot, abbreviated P2TR, is the output kind of segwit version 1. For a P2TR output the witness program is a point on the secp256k1 curve. The book says that it may be a simple public key, but that in most cases it should be a public key that commits to some additional data, a commitment explained in a later chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The output script is OP_1 followed by the 32-byte program, and the address uses bech32m (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Pay to taproot, abbreviated P2TR, is the output kind of segwit version 1. For a P2TR output the witness program is a point on the secp256k1 curve. The book says that it may be a simple public key, but that in most cases it should be a public key that commits to some additional data, a commitment explained in a later chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The output script is OP_1 followed by the 32-byte program, and the address uses bech32m (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Taproot gives a single output the flexibility to be spent either by a signature from one key or by revealing conditions that were committed to in the key. The program is only 32 bytes because the signature standard that goes with it, the Schnorr signatures of BIP340, encodes public keys as 32 bytes, instead of the 33-byte compressed encodings that are common in Bitcoin today (Wuille et al., 2020). Signatures take a fixed 64 bytes in this scheme (Wuille et al., 2020).

The book's example program is 2ceefa5fa770ff24f87c5475d76eab519eda6176b11dbe1618fcf755bfac5311 and its address is bc1p9nh05ha8wrljf7ru236awm4t2x0d5ctkkywmu9sclnm4t0av2vgs4k3au7. Bitcoin Core 31.1 reports the address as valid, of witness version 1 with that program (Bitcoin Core, 2026). When the same key is given to Core as the internal key of a tr descriptor, the address differs, because the descriptor language defines the argument of tr as the internal key from which the output key is made, while a descriptor called rawtr takes the key as it is (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A 32-byte x coordinate stands for a point because the curve equation determines y up to its sign, and the Schnorr standard settles the sign by convention: the point with an even y coordinate is taken (Wuille et al., 2020). The chapter's checks confirm that the book's program is a valid x coordinate, by computing a square root of x cubed plus 7 and testing that it satisfies the equation, and that the toolkit's bech32m encoding of the program gives the book's address.

A taproot address commits to a key, not to a hash of a key, so the key is visible in the output from the start; the benefit of a hash hiding the key until spending is traded for flexibility and smaller signatures. The book returns to the topic in a later chapter, and this chapter treats it only as an output kind that needs a bech32m address.

nodes.definition: A P2TR output script is OP_1 followed by a 32-byte witness program that is a point on the secp256k1 curve, which may be a public key or a key that commits to more data; its address is bech32m.

nodes.label: Practice
nodes.body: This branch asks what a user or a developer should do with the material of the earlier branches today. The chapter ends with advanced keys and addresses, vanity addresses and paper wallets, and it surrounds them with remarks about how practice has changed since the first Bitcoin software. The branch collects those remarks together with the current behaviour of Bitcoin Core, which was run for this chapter, and with the way in which implementers can convince themselves that their address code is correct.

paras.text: This branch asks what a user or a developer should do with the material of the earlier branches today. The chapter ends with advanced keys and addresses, vanity addresses and paper wallets, and it surrounds them with remarks about how practice has changed since the first Bitcoin software. The branch collects those remarks together with the current behaviour of Bitcoin Core, which was run for this chapter, and with the way in which implementers can convince themselves that their address code is correct.

A chapter of a book is a snapshot, and software moves on. The book says of private key formats that the information is mainly of interest to anyone needing compatibility with early Bitcoin wallets, because modern wallets generate all their keys from one seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A student who learns only the formats of the early years may look for features that current software has removed. The branch therefore compares what the book says with what a recent release of Bitcoin Core does, and where they differ it says so.

The material is met by anyone who installs a wallet, restores a backup, imports an old key or writes software that pays addresses. Chapter 3 described how to obtain, verify and run Bitcoin Core and its interface; this chapter used a release of it, version 31.1, as an independent authority on addresses, by asking it to derive and to validate every address that the book prints.

Two levels organise the branch. The first, practice now, covers the default address type of a current wallet, the export of single keys, the protection of a key with a passphrase, the deterministic wallet that has replaced single keys, the privacy cost of reusing an address, the vanity address, the paper wallet and the hardware device that has replaced it. The second level, assurance, covers the test vectors of the standards and the habit of checking an implementation against independent software.

Practice is not static. A statement of the form wallets do X is true of some wallets at some date; the dates attached to the sources in this chapter, a book of 2023 and software of 2026, are part of the information. Where a source and the software disagree, the software of the date is the better witness to what happens now, and the source the better witness to what its authors intended.

nodes.label: Practice now
nodes.body: Practice now means the behaviour of current wallets and the advice of the book's third edition. It covers which address a wallet gives out, whether a wallet still lets a user take a single key out of it, how keys are protected, and which of the curiosities of the early years, vanity addresses and paper wallets, are still sensible. The book is blunt about several of them, calling paper wallets obsolete and dangerous and observing that vanity addresses have almost entirely disappeared (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Practice now means the behaviour of current wallets and the advice of the book's third edition. It covers which address a wallet gives out, whether a wallet still lets a user take a single key out of it, how keys are protected, and which of the curiosities of the early years, vanity addresses and paper wallets, are still sensible. The book is blunt about several of them, calling paper wallets obsolete and dangerous and observing that vanity addresses have almost entirely disappeared (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Learning the current practice protects against mistakes that came from earlier habits. The old way of keeping bitcoins, one key per address, each backed up on paper or in a file, led to lost keys and to leaked keys. The modern way derives all the keys of a wallet from a single seed, which can be backed up once, and this changes what exporting a key, protecting a key and printing a key mean.

The eight concepts of the level move from the wallet outward. The default address type and the export of a single key say what current software offers. Passphrase protection, the deterministic wallet and address reuse explain the surrounding security and privacy ideas. The vanity address, the paper wallet and the hardware signing device are three ways of obtaining or keeping a key, one of them fashionable in the early years and abandoned, one obsolete, and one recommended.

A recommendation in this level is the authors' judgement at a date, and the book frames them so: the paper wallet section is a warning rather than a procedure, and the section on key formats says in its own words that it is mainly of interest to anyone needing compatibility with early wallets. The reader should keep the facts apart from the opinions and should check the date of any advice before acting on it. The facts of this level are of two kinds, and they age differently: what a document says, which stays true of that document for ever, and what a program does, which is true of one release on one day.

nodes.label: Default address type
nodes.body: The default address type is the kind of address that a wallet gives out when the user does not ask for another. In Bitcoin Core it is controlled by the option addresstype, whose help text lists the possible values as legacy, p2sh-segwit, bech32 and bech32m, with the default bech32 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The command getnewaddress accepts the same four values as its address type argument, and its default is whatever the option sets (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The default address type is the kind of address that a wallet gives out when the user does not ask for another. In Bitcoin Core it is controlled by the option addresstype, whose help text lists the possible values as legacy, p2sh-segwit, bech32 and bech32m, with the default bech32 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The command getnewaddress accepts the same four values as its address type argument, and its default is whatever the option sets (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A default shapes what most users do. The default of the reference implementation tells the whole ecosystem which address format is regarded as current, and the book supports the choice when it calls bech32m the current recommended address format for wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Defaults also matter for compatibility: a payer's wallet must be able to pay whatever kind the receiver's wallet hands out.

The chapter's evidence is a run of Bitcoin Core 31.1 as an offline node with a new wallet. The default address was a bech32 address, a P2WPKH output of witness version 0; asking for the types legacy, p2sh-segwit, bech32 and bech32m produced a P2PKH address, a P2SH address of a P2WPKH script, a P2WPKH address, and a P2TR address of witness version 1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The first three names correspond to the kinds of this chapter that carry a single key, and the fourth, as the name says, uses bech32m.

The wallet reports the kind of each address through its descriptor, the output descriptor of Chapter 3: wpkh for the default and the bech32 type, pkh for the legacy type, sh for the nested type, and tr for the bech32m type (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chapter's checks read these facts from the saved output of the run and also test the book's claim about the version numbers, finding witness version 0 for the first two segwit kinds and 1 for the taproot kind.

A default is not a rule. Another wallet may default to another kind, and the choice of the kind of address for a payment belongs to the receiver, who makes it known by the address itself; a payer never chooses it. A default also says nothing about which kinds a wallet can pay, which is a separate question and the one that decided the design of bech32. Note finally that the evidence here concerns one release on one date, release 31.1 as it was run for this chapter, while the book was printed in 2023 and describes the practice of that year.

nodes.example: bech32 by default, bech32m on request
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core's addresstype option defaults to bech32, a P2WPKH address, and the four types are legacy, p2sh-segwit, bech32 and bech32m, the last a taproot address.

nodes.label: Exporting a single key
nodes.body: Exporting a single key means taking one private key out of a wallet, usually as a wallet import format string, so that it can be put into another wallet. It was an everyday operation of the early wallets, which held independent keys, and Bitcoin Core offered the commands dumpprivkey to export a key and importprivkey to import one. The book says that almost no modern wallets support the ability to export or import an individual key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Exporting a single key means taking one private key out of a wallet, usually as a wallet import format string, so that it can be put into another wallet. It was an everyday operation of the early wallets, which held independent keys, and Bitcoin Core offered the commands dumpprivkey to export a key and importprivkey to import one. The book says that almost no modern wallets support the ability to export or import an individual key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reason is the deterministic wallet. The book explains that if a user exports a single private key from such a wallet and an attacker obtains that key together with some nonprivate data about the wallet, the attacker can potentially derive any private key in the wallet, which allows the theft of all the funds; and that keys cannot be imported into deterministic wallets at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The operation that was routine for independent keys is dangerous and often impossible for derived ones.

Bitcoin Core followed the change. The release notes of version 30.0 state that BDB legacy wallets, that is the ones kept in a Berkeley DB file, can no longer be created or loaded and list among the removed legacy-only commands dumpprivkey, importprivkey, dumpwallet and importmulti (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In the chapter's run of release 31.1 the help for both dumpprivkey and importprivkey answered unknown command (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A key can still be brought in through the descriptor interface. The command importdescriptors imports descriptors, and the help text warns that it triggers a rescan of the blockchain and requires a new wallet backup (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A descriptor can contain a wallet import format string: given the descriptors pkh and wpkh with the book's WIF strings, Bitcoin Core returned the P2PKH addresses 1424C2F4bC9JidNjjTUZCbUxv6Sa1Mt62x for the uncompressed string and 1J7mdg5rbQyUHENYdx39WVWK7fsLpEoXZy for the compressed one, and the P2WPKH address bc1qh0q7g23e6pdye3sh2ttfvwmld8gfhvnmmfxuck, the addresses that the chapter computes by hand (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The course material that accompanies this chapter describes the earlier workflow: to ask the node to expose a private key one used the dumpprivkey command, and its example prints the address 1J7mdg5rbQyUHENYdx39WVWK7fsLpEoXZy from getnewaddress and then the compressed wallet import format string of that address from dumpprivkey (Altunel, 2021). That workflow no longer works in a current Bitcoin Core, though the first command is still present (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A key that has been exported, even by a legacy wallet that still allows it, is a copy of the secret and must be treated like the secret itself; the loss of control of the copy is the loss of control of the funds.

nodes.definition: Deterministic descriptor wallets no longer export single keys, and Bitcoin Core removed dumpprivkey and importprivkey in 30.0, while a WIF key can still be used inside a descriptor.

nodes.label: Passphrase-protected key
nodes.body: Passphrase protection is the encryption of a private key under a passphrase, a secret phrase chosen by the owner, so that the key can be stored or printed without being usable by whoever finds it. BIP38 specifies how: it proposes a method of encrypting and encoding a passphrase-protected private key record as a 58-character base58check string (Caldwell and Voisine, 2012). The record contains everything needed to reconstitute the private key except the passphrase.

paras.text: Passphrase protection is the encryption of a private key under a passphrase, a secret phrase chosen by the owner, so that the key can be stored or printed without being usable by whoever finds it. BIP38 specifies how: it proposes a method of encrypting and encoding a passphrase-protected private key record as a 58-character base58check string (Caldwell and Voisine, 2012). The record contains everything needed to reconstitute the private key except the passphrase.

The proposal was written for paper wallets and physical bitcoins. Its motivation is a two-factor arrangement, something you have plus something you know: a person holding the printed record cannot spend without the passphrase, and the passphrase can be sent through another channel, for instance the telephone, while the record goes by post (Caldwell and Voisine, 2012). The third edition of the book does not cover the format at all, whereas the course material that accompanies this chapter, written on the second edition, presents it: there BIP38 is described as a common standard for encrypting private keys with a passphrase and encoding them with base58check, so that they can be stored on backup media or transported between wallets, with the Advanced Encryption Standard named as the cipher (Altunel, 2021).

The BIPs repository gives BIP38 the status Deployed, yet the summary of the comments on it reads Unanimously Discourage for implementation (Caldwell and Voisine, 2012). The two statements are compatible: the format exists and is in use, and those who commented advise against building it into new software. The format is therefore of interest for old paper wallets and encrypted keys that someone may still hold.

The encryption uses three tools. The passphrase is stretched into a key by scrypt, a key derivation function that is deliberately slow and memory-hungry in order to resist brute-force attacks. The 32-byte private key is then encrypted with AES, a widely used block cipher, in two halves of 16 bytes. The first four bytes of the double SHA256 of the Bitcoin address serve as a salt for scrypt and as a check that the passphrase was right (Caldwell and Voisine, 2012). The result is encoded in base58check with the 2-byte prefix 0x0142 for a record without EC multiplication, followed by 37 further bytes; the specification publishes the first and the last of the 2 to the 296 possible strings of each kind, and the chapter's checks reproduce the first, 6PRHv1jg1ytiE4kT2QtrUz8gEjMQghZDWg1FuxjdYDzjUkcJeGdFj9q9Vi, from the bytes 01 42 C0 and thirty-six zeros with the base58check procedure of the toolkit.

A passphrase adds protection only if it is not guessable, and the scrypt step only slows a guesser down; it does not stop one. The extra factor also adds a new way to lose funds: forget the passphrase, and the key is gone. As the book asks readers to use a recovery code and a hardware signing device instead of printed keys, the format is mainly a matter of compatibility (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: BIP38 encrypts a private key under a passphrase into a 58-character base58check string starting with 6P; the BIPs repository lists it as Deployed with the comment summary Unanimously Discourage for implementation, and the 3rd edition does not cover it.

nodes.label: Deterministic wallet and seed
nodes.body: A deterministic wallet is a wallet whose private keys are all derived from a single random value, called the seed, by a procedure that always gives the same results for the same seed. The book of this course shows the idea with a hash function: if the seed is hashed together with the numbers 0, 1 and 2, three seemingly random values come out, and using the same hash function with the same seed always gives the same values (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book says that a user of deterministic key generation can back up every key in the wallet by simply recording the seed and a reference to the algorithm used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A deterministic wallet is a wallet whose private keys are all derived from a single random value, called the seed, by a procedure that always gives the same results for the same seed. The book of this course shows the idea with a hash function: if the seed is hashed together with the numbers 0, 1 and 2, three seemingly random values come out, and using the same hash function with the same seed always gives the same values (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book says that a user of deterministic key generation can back up every key in the wallet by simply recording the seed and a reference to the algorithm used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The earlier arrangement, in which a wallet generated independent keys, needed a new backup every time a new key was generated or imported. The fourth chapter's section on key formats says that later wallets began to use deterministic wallets, which only ever need to be backed up once for typical use on the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This is also why Chapter 1's recovery code can be a short list of words: it encodes the seed from which everything else follows.

Almost all current wallets are of this type. The consequences for this chapter are the ones that the book draws: a single exported key can endanger the others, keys cannot be imported, and a vanity address, which comes from a separate search, does not fit into the scheme unless the user backs up additional data for it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The more elaborate hierarchical form, with a tree of keys derived from one seed, is the subject of the next chapter.

The book's own demonstration reproduces exactly. The seed is the hexadecimal text f1cc3bc0 and so on, the derived values are the SHA256 of the text 'seed + i' with a line break, and the three results begin 50b18e0b, a965dbcd and 19580c97. The chapter's checks recompute them with the hash function of the standard library. Real wallets use a stronger and more structured derivation than a bare hash, but the principle is the same: the keys are a function of the seed, so protecting the seed protects the keys, and losing the seed loses them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The seed is a single point of failure in both directions: whoever obtains it can generate every private key and steal all the funds, and whoever loses it loses them all. The book says exactly that of the seed and its recovery code: someone else who gets the seed can generate all of the private keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A reader should therefore keep the idea of the deterministic wallet apart from the idea of backup: derivation makes the backup short, but it does not make it safe.

nodes.definition: A deterministic wallet derives all its private keys from a single seed, a random value, by a repeatable procedure, so one backup covers every key; the book's example derives three keys by hashing the seed with 0, 1 and 2.

nodes.label: Address reuse and privacy
nodes.body: Address reuse is the practice of receiving more than one payment to the same address. Because all the transactions are public, every payment to an address is visible together with every other payment to it. The book makes the point about vanity addresses: using a vanity address to receive multiple payments to the same address creates a link between all of those payments (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Address reuse is the practice of receiving more than one payment to the same address. Because all the transactions are public, every payment to an address is visible together with every other payment to it. The book makes the point about vanity addresses: using a vanity address to receive multiple payments to the same address creates a link between all of those payments (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The link matters for people other than the receiver. The book gives two small stories: Alice may want to donate anonymously, and Bob may not want his other customers to know that he gives discount pricing to the charity (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same reasoning stands behind the first design of Bitcoin, in which the receiver's node supplied a new public key that it had never previously given anyone, so that different payments to Bob could not be connected by someone looking at the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Wallets avoid the problem by giving a new address for every payment, which is cheap when all the keys derive from one seed. The default behaviour of Bitcoin Core's command getnewaddress is exactly that: a new address on every call (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Reuse is still met when a person publishes one address on a website or a poster, and with the vanity address, whose point is to be recognised.

The link is created by the observer, not by the protocol. Anyone can scan the blockchain for outputs to the same address and list the payments, the amounts and the dates. A fresh address splits the history into pieces that have nothing visible in common. The chapter's checks illustrate the principle with a set: three payments to one address give one distinct address, three payments to three addresses give three.

A fresh address for each payment does not give anonymity by itself, and the book is careful in its claims: it says that the reuse of a vanity address reduces privacy, not that avoiding reuse guarantees it. Reuse may be acceptable when a link is wanted anyway, as the book remarks for a non-profit that reports its income and expenditure to a tax authority (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The public key behind an address is also exposed when the address is first spent from, which gives one more reason to treat each address as single-use.

nodes.definition: Receiving several payments to the same address links them all together for anyone looking at the blockchain, which reduces the privacy of everyone who pays or is paid by that address.

nodes.label: Vanity address
nodes.body: A vanity address is a valid Bitcoin address that contains a human-readable message, such as the address 1LoveBPzzD72PUXLzCkYAtGFYmK5vYNR33 of the book, whose first four base58 letters after the digit 1 spell Love (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Such addresses are not designed but searched for: the process picks a private key at random, derives the public key and the address, checks whether it matches the wanted pattern, and repeats billions of times until a match is found (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A vanity address is a valid Bitcoin address that contains a human-readable message, such as the address 1LoveBPzzD72PUXLzCkYAtGFYmK5vYNR33 of the book, whose first four base58 letters after the digit 1 spell Love (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Such addresses are not designed but searched for: the process picks a private key at random, derives the public key and the address, checks whether it matches the wanted pattern, and repeats billions of times until a match is found (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The attraction is recognition; the book's example is a children's charity that wants an address beginning 1Kids to publicise a fundraising drive. The cost is computing time. The book is clear that the result is no less and no more secure than any other address: the key that was found spends the funds like any key, it depends on the same elliptic curve cryptography and the same secure hash algorithm, and one cannot find the private key of a vanity address more easily than that of another (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book reports that vanity addresses were popular in the early years of Bitcoin but have almost entirely disappeared from use as of 2023, and it names two likely causes. Deterministic wallets make it impossible to use a vanity address unless the user backs up additional data for each one, and most such wallets do not allow the import of a key from a vanity generator. And address reuse, which a vanity address invites, reduces privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A vanity pool is a service that lets those with fast hardware earn bitcoin searching for vanity addresses for others (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book counts the work. An address with the prefix 1Kids lies in a range of about 58 to the 29, that is 1.4 times 10 to the 51, addresses; each further character of the pattern makes the pattern 58 times rarer, so that the frequencies run 1 in 58, 1 in 3,364 and 1 in 195,000 for patterns of one, two and three characters after the 1, and 1 in 11 million for four (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's checks recompute these powers of 58 for one to eleven characters. They also run a real, small search, counting private keys upwards from 1: the first key whose compressed P2PKH address begins with 1Ki is the number 1666, and the first that begins with 1Kid is the number 8810. The number of tries depends on luck, and these are far below the averages.

The search is a brute-force one and it multiplies its cost by 58 for every character, so long patterns are out of reach: the book says that a pattern such as 1KidsCharity would take 2.5 million years on a desktop computer. Its table of times follows its own rule, half the frequency divided by 100,000 keys a second, up to patterns of seven characters, but for eight and more characters the book's times are about a third shorter than the rule gives, and its frequency for eleven characters, 23 quintillion, should be 25 quintillion according to the powers of 58, as the chapter's checks show. The examples that this chapter found, with keys 1666 and 8810, also give a warning: a key found by counting upwards from 1 is not secret at all, and a real search must draw its candidate keys at random.

nodes.definition: A vanity address starts with a chosen string found by trying keys one after another, and each further character multiplies the work by 58, so four characters take 58 to the fourth, about 11 million keys.

nodes.label: Paper wallet
nodes.body: A paper wallet is a private key printed on paper, often together with the corresponding Bitcoin address for convenience, though this is not necessary, because the address can be derived from the private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book shows a sample and describes many designs: some for gifts, with seasonal themes; some for storage in a bank vault with the key hidden by a scratch-off sticker or by tamper-proof foil; some with detachable stubs that allow several copies to be kept against fire or flood (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A paper wallet is a private key printed on paper, often together with the corresponding Bitcoin address for convenience, though this is not necessary, because the address can be derived from the private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book shows a sample and describes many designs: some for gifts, with seasonal themes; some for storage in a bank vault with the key hidden by a scratch-off sticker or by tamper-proof foil; some with detachable stubs that allow several copies to be kept against fire or flood (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A wallet on paper was an answer to the question of how to keep a key away from computers that can be attacked. The book now declares the answer wrong. Paper wallets are an obsolete technology and dangerous for most users, there are many subtle pitfalls in generating them, not least that the generating code might be compromised with a back door, and many bitcoins have been stolen in this way; they are shown for informational purposes only and should not be used for storing bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book recommends the alternative in the same warning: use a recovery code to back up the keys, possibly with a hardware signing device to store keys and sign transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A paper wallet is met mainly in old gifts and old backups, and the reader who finds one should treat the printed key like any other private key, in the format described by the wallet import format.

A paper wallet has to be generated by software, which chooses the random number and prints the key; the worked example counts what then has to be printed and kept safe, namely 64 hexadecimal digits, which are the 32 bytes of the private key. The security of the paper therefore depends first on that software and on the randomness it used, the issue of the earlier concepts on randomness, and only afterwards on where the paper is kept. Two risks follow: the software is not trusted, and the paper, once read or photographed, is a complete copy of the secret.

The recommendation against paper wallets is a statement about generation and about the format of a single static key, and not about writing things on paper: the recovery code of a modern wallet is routinely written on paper, and the book proposes exactly this. The difference is that a recovery code can regenerate a whole wallet from a trustworthy device, and a paper wallet is one key produced by a program whose trustworthiness the owner cannot check.

nodes.definition: A paper wallet is a private key printed on paper, which the 3rd edition calls an obsolete technology and dangerous for most users.

nodes.label: Hardware signing device
nodes.body: A hardware signing device is a small device whose only job is to hold private keys and to use them to generate signatures. The book of this course describes it in the chapter on wallets: Alice gives a hardware signing device, sometimes confusingly called a hardware wallet, the key tweaks she needs, the device derives the child private keys and signs the transaction, and it returns the signed transaction to the less secure frontend for broadcast to the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A hardware signing device is a small device whose only job is to hold private keys and to use them to generate signatures. The book of this course describes it in the chapter on wallets: Alice gives a hardware signing device, sometimes confusingly called a hardware wallet, the key tweaks she needs, the device derives the child private keys and signs the transaction, and it returns the signed transaction to the less secure frontend for broadcast to the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A computer or phone runs a great deal of software of unknown quality, and a key that is held there can be stolen by it. Another chapter of the book states the idea in general terms: unlike a smartphone or desktop computer, a hardware signing device only needs to hold keys and use them to generate signatures, and without general-purpose software to compromise and with limited interfaces such devices can deliver strong security to nonexpert users (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It adds that they may become the predominant method of storing bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

This chapter meets the device twice. The multisignature example of P2SH, a signature from Bob's desktop wallet and one from a hardware signing device, shows it as one of the keys of a script, and the warning against paper wallets recommends it, with a recovery code, as the replacement (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The device is therefore a place where keys are kept, and not a new kind of address.

The division of labour is the point. The frontend, which can be an ordinary program, builds the transaction and shows it; the device checks it, signs it with the key it keeps inside and sends back only the signature. The worked example names the three steps in order and asks whether the private key is among them, and it is not: preparing and broadcasting happen outside the device, signing inside it, and the key never appears in the list of things that cross the boundary. Since a signature does not reveal the private key, the key is never exposed to the frontend, however compromised the frontend is (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The device still needs the secret to be backed up, so a recovery code, as the book says, goes with it.

A hardware signing device is not magic. It protects keys from software on the computer, not from loss, so the recovery code must still be kept, and not from the owner's own mistakes, such as signing a transaction that pays the wrong address. The name hardware wallet is called confusing by the book because the device does not hold coins; it holds keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: keys that never leave the device
nodes.definition: A hardware signing device holds private keys and uses them only to sign; a less secure program prepares the transaction and broadcasts it, so the keys never meet general-purpose software.

nodes.label: Assurance
nodes.body: Assurance is the confidence that an implementation does what the standard says. In a payment system an implementation error is not a minor bug: an address decoder that accepts a string it should reject, or encodes a program wrongly, sends money to a place from which it cannot be recovered. This level of the chapter covers the two means that the chapter itself uses to obtain assurance, the published test vectors of the address standards and the comparison of independent implementations.

paras.text: Assurance is the confidence that an implementation does what the standard says. In a payment system an implementation error is not a minor bug: an address decoder that accepts a string it should reject, or encodes a program wrongly, sends money to a place from which it cannot be recovered. This level of the chapter covers the two means that the chapter itself uses to obtain assurance, the published test vectors of the address standards and the comparison of independent implementations.

The book asks directly for such assurance. When implementing bech32m encoding or decoding, it says, use the test vectors provided in BIP350, and make sure the code passes the vectors for paying future segwit versions that have not yet been defined, so that the software remains usable for many years (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The specification itself explains why: experiments on implementations of the earlier format found that many wallets and services did not support sending to higher-version outputs (Wuille, 2020).

Assurance works by comparing a program against something that was not produced by that program. A test vector does this by fixing an input and the answer the standard requires, so that an implementation which disagrees is wrong by definition rather than by opinion; vectors that cover cases the implementer did not think of - strings that must be rejected, versions not yet defined - are the valuable ones, because they test the boundaries where an implementation silently guesses. A cross-check does it by running two implementations written by different people on the same input and comparing, which catches a shared misreading of the standard only when the two authors read it independently. Neither method proves a program correct: both are ways of raising the cost of being wrong, and the published record of wallets that could not pay the newer addresses is what that cost looks like when nobody pays it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2020).

The reader meets assurance in this course as a habit rather than a topic. Every figure in this chapter is recomputed before it is stated, and where a standard publishes a vector the computation is run against the vector; where an independent program is available, the answer is asked of it as well, which for this chapter meant putting the derivations to a real release of the reference implementation. The same habit appears in the chapter's own record of findings, where a statement of the book that did not survive the check is written down with what the sources actually say (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is that passing the vectors is a floor and not a ceiling. A decoder can agree with every published example and still mishandle an input nobody published; an implementation can be right about the arithmetic and wrong about where it keeps the key. And a cross-check between two programs that share a library is not independent, however separate the programs look, which is worth remembering whenever two tools agree suspiciously quickly (Wuille, 2020).

nodes.label: BIP350 test vectors
nodes.body: A test vector is an input together with the output that a correct implementation must give, published so that implementers can check their work. BIP350 publishes three groups: valid bech32m strings, invalid bech32m strings with the reason for the invalidity, and valid and invalid segwit addresses of versions 0 to 16, the valid ones with the output script that they translate to (Wuille, 2020). The chapter's checks count seven valid bech32m strings, eight valid segwit addresses and fifteen invalid ones.

paras.text: A test vector is an input together with the output that a correct implementation must give, published so that implementers can check their work. BIP350 publishes three groups: valid bech32m strings, invalid bech32m strings with the reason for the invalidity, and valid and invalid segwit addresses of versions 0 to 16, the valid ones with the output script that they translate to (Wuille, 2020). The chapter's checks count seven valid bech32m strings, eight valid segwit addresses and fifteen invalid ones.

Vectors capture the cases that implementers forget. The invalid list contains an address with the wrong human-readable part, a checksum of the wrong kind for the version, a version out of range, a program that is too short or too long, mixed case, and padding errors, each with the reason. The valid list contains addresses of the versions that did not yet exist, so that wallets are forward-compatible. The specification says that all higher versions of native segwit outputs should be recognised as valid recipients, while no wallet should ever create them (Wuille, 2020).

The book recommends the vectors twice, once for the encoding rules and once for the future versions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's own toolkit was run against them, and it accepted all eight valid addresses with the right scripts and rejected all fifteen invalid ones, as did the reference implementation that the book uses. This is the kind of evidence the book asks implementers to produce.

A vector test is a loop. For each valid address the decoder must return the stated witness version and program, and re-encoding must give the same address in lowercase; for each invalid address it must refuse. The checks of this chapter read the vectors from the saved text of the specification, parse the groups and run the toolkit's decoder on each; they also confirm that none of the bech32m strings is accepted when read as bech32 (Wuille, 2020).

Passing the vectors is necessary but not sufficient: they sample the space of inputs and do not cover it. A decoder that passes can still contain a bug for a case that none of the vectors tries, so vectors should be combined with the other checks of the next concept, and with careful reading of the specification.

nodes.example: BIP350's list of valid and invalid addresses
nodes.definition: The BIP350 test vectors give valid and invalid segwit addresses and bech32m strings against which any bech32m implementation should be run, including those for future witness versions.

nodes.label: Cross-checking with independent software
nodes.body: Cross-checking is the comparison of the results of independent implementations on the same inputs. If a toolkit written by one person and a program written by others, without sharing code, give the same answer for many inputs, the chance that both have the same error is much smaller than the chance that one has an error. The chapter applies the method to its main example: the private key of the book, with its public key, its two P2PKH addresses and its two WIF strings.

paras.text: Cross-checking is the comparison of the results of independent implementations on the same inputs. If a toolkit written by one person and a program written by others, without sharing code, give the same answer for many inputs, the chance that both have the same error is much smaller than the chance that one has an error. The chapter applies the method to its main example: the private key of the book, with its public key, its two P2PKH addresses and its two WIF strings.

The method is the way in which trust is built in this field, by checking that several independent implementations agree and not by believing one. The book itself relies on it when it advises readers not to write their own code for random numbers, and the specifications publish reference implementations, so that others can compare. Where an implementation is for teaching, as the toolkit of this chapter is, the comparison is the only reason to believe its output.

Three sources were compared. The toolkit of the chapter, written for reading in plain Python, computed the public key, the two addresses and the two WIF strings of the book's key. Bitcoin Core 31.1, given the public keys and the WIF strings in descriptors, returned the same two P2PKH addresses and a P2WPKH address, and validated every address that the chapter prints (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The reference implementation of bech32 that the book itself uses produced the same four segwit addresses as the toolkit.

The procedure is simple. Fix the inputs, in this case the 64 hexadecimal digits of the key; run each implementation; compare outputs exactly, character by character. Disagreement points to an error in at least one of them. The chapter's checks recompute the toolkit's outputs and compare them with the saved output of Bitcoin Core, and they check the error positions that Core reports against the positions at which the typed string differs from the correct address.

Agreement shows that the results are the same, not that they are right: two programs can agree on a mistake if they share a source of error, such as a misreading of the same specification. The comparison also covers only the inputs tried. The chapter's differences from the book, such as the statement about the origin of secp256k1 and the figures of the vanity table, were found by comparing the book with primary sources, which is a cross-check of another kind.

nodes.definition: Cross-checking compares the results of independent implementations on the same input; this chapter compares its own toolkit with Bitcoin Core 31.1 and with the book's reference code, and finds the same addresses.

nodes.label: Semantics
nodes.body: This branch links the chapter to the theme of the course on identity and semantics. A key pair, as the chapter has described it, is more than a means of paying: it is an identifier whose holder can prove control without asking anyone. That is the property around which the W3C's Decentralized Identifiers are designed, and the branch explains the connection and uses it to name the ideas of the chapter in terms that are used outside Bitcoin.

paras.text: This branch links the chapter to the theme of the course on identity and semantics. A key pair, as the chapter has described it, is more than a means of paying: it is an identifier whose holder can prove control without asking anyone. That is the property around which the W3C's Decentralized Identifiers are designed, and the branch explains the connection and uses it to name the ideas of the chapter in terms that are used outside Bitcoin.

Bitcoin's keys are often discussed as money. Seen as identifiers, they raise questions about how a name for something can be created, recognised and proved without a central registry. Chapter 1 introduced the idea of decentralized identity in connection with Bitcoin addresses, and this branch says what precisely makes a key pair suitable for it: the holder of the private key can sign, anyone can verify, and nobody has to grant permission.

The branch has one level, identifiers, with three concepts. The first is the proof of control by a key, the cryptographic property from which the rest follows. The second is the uniform resource identifier, the kind of name that web standards use. The third is the decentralized identifier, a specific standard that combines a name of that kind with public keys.

A resemblance is not an identity. Bitcoin addresses and decentralized identifiers share a design idea, but they are different things with different specifications, and no part of Bitcoin is a decentralized identifier method simply by being a key pair. There are methods that do use a blockchain, and there are methods that use none, and whether any of them uses Bitcoin is a question about that method and not about Bitcoin. The branch therefore states only what the two sets of sources say, keeps the two vocabularies apart, and leaves the comparison as a comparison.

nodes.label: Identifiers
nodes.body: An identifier is a name that refers to a thing, so that statements about the thing can be made, stored and found. A public key can be used as such a name, because a key pair lets its holder show, by a signature, that a statement comes from the one who holds the matching private key. This level of the chapter gathers the concepts that connect key pairs to the identifier standards of the web.

paras.text: An identifier is a name that refers to a thing, so that statements about the thing can be made, stored and found. A public key can be used as such a name, because a key pair lets its holder show, by a signature, that a statement comes from the one who holds the matching private key. This level of the chapter gathers the concepts that connect key pairs to the identifier standards of the web.

Identifiers matter wherever data from different sources must be linked. In the semantic web, a thing is named by an identifier that is unique and that others can use. Most identifiers depend on a central authority, which assigns names and can withdraw them. A name that its holder controls by a key does not need such an authority, and the question that the standards pose is how to describe and discover the keys behind a name.

The ladder works by separating three questions that are easy to run together: what a name is, who may issue it, and how a claim made under it is checked. A uniform resource identifier answers the first by fixing a syntax, so that the same string denotes the same thing in every program that reads it. The usual answer to the second is an authority - a registry that assigns the name and can take it back - and the identifiers of this section replace that authority with a key: the name contains, or resolves to, a document naming the public keys whose holder controls it, so issuing the name needs nobody's permission and control is demonstrated rather than recorded. The third question is answered by a signature, which anyone holding the public key can check and nobody else can produce. A Bitcoin key pair supplies exactly that third piece and nothing more, which is why it maps onto one field of such a document - a verification method - rather than onto the identifier as a whole (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022) (Berners-Lee et al., 2005).

The reader meets this level wherever data from two systems has to be joined. Within this course it is met in the semantic branch of each chapter, where a concept, a source and a finding each carry an identifier so that a statement about one can be stored and found; outside it, in any catalogue that must refer to records it does not own. The identifiers that a key controls are met in practice in credential systems, where the holder of a name proves control at the moment of use instead of relying on a directory that may be offline or mistaken (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022) (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

The caution is that a key proves control and nothing else. It does not say who the controller is, that the controller is the person they claim to be, or that the key has not changed hands; a document naming keys is only as current as whoever last updated it. And Bitcoin's own identifiers are not of this family: an address is a commitment to a spending condition, not a name with a document behind it, and a learner who treats the two as the same thing will expect a resolution step that Bitcoin does not have (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

nodes.label: Proof of control by a key
nodes.body: Proof of control by a key is the act of showing that one holds a private key without revealing it, by producing a signature that others can verify with the public key. The book describes the property: a signature can only be produced by someone with knowledge of the private key, yet anyone with the public key and the transaction can verify it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nothing in the procedure requires the verifier to ask a third party.

paras.text: Proof of control by a key is the act of showing that one holds a private key without revealing it, by producing a signature that others can verify with the public key. The book describes the property: a signature can only be produced by someone with knowledge of the private key, yet anyone with the public key and the transaction can verify it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nothing in the procedure requires the verifier to ask a third party.

This is what makes a key suitable as the basis of an identity that nobody grants. Ownership of bitcoins is exactly proof of control: a node accepts a spend because the signature verifies against the public key to which the funds were paid, not because anybody vouches for the spender. The identity of the spender is not needed; control is enough, which is the privacy aim with which the chapter began (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The property is met in every Bitcoin transaction, and outside Bitcoin in the login procedures and certificates that rest on public key cryptography. In the Decentralized Identifiers specification the same idea appears as the ability of the controller of an identifier to prove control over it without requiring permission from any other party (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

To prove control the holder signs a challenge: a message that the verifier chooses, so that an old signature cannot be replayed. The verifier checks the signature against the public key. The chapter's checks apply the toolkit's ECDSA sketch to the book's key: a signature of a message verifies against the public key, and the same signature does not verify against a different message or a different key. The sketch signs a message hash with a nonce that the caller supplies, which a real signer must not do.

Proof of control is not proof of identity. It shows that the prover holds the key, not who the prover is, and not that the key is the one the verifier meant: the binding of a key to a person or an organisation needs something further, such as a document from a trusted source. A key whose private part has been stolen proves control for the thief.

nodes.definition: Whoever holds a private key can prove control of the matching public key by signing, without a central registry or anyone's permission.

nodes.label: Uniform resource identifier (URI)
nodes.body: A Uniform Resource Identifier, abbreviated URI, is a compact sequence of characters that identifies an abstract or physical resource. The specification of URIs, RFC 3986, defines the generic syntax and a process for resolving URI references, and its grammar allows an implementation to parse the common components of a URI without knowing the requirements of every particular kind of identifier (Berners-Lee et al., 2005). A web address is a URI, and so is the payment request address of Chapter 2, whose scheme is bitcoin.

paras.text: A Uniform Resource Identifier, abbreviated URI, is a compact sequence of characters that identifies an abstract or physical resource. The specification of URIs, RFC 3986, defines the generic syntax and a process for resolving URI references, and its grammar allows an implementation to parse the common components of a URI without knowing the requirements of every particular kind of identifier (Berners-Lee et al., 2005). A web address is a URI, and so is the payment request address of Chapter 2, whose scheme is bitcoin.

A URI gives a thing a name that machines can handle, store, compare and send: the same string refers to the same resource wherever it appears. The semantic technologies of the course rest on this property, since statements are made about resources named by identifiers, and the DID standard chose to be a URI in order to fit into that world. Chapter 3 introduced the IRI, the variant of the URI that allows international characters.

The identifiers of the DID standard are URIs. The example of the specification is did:example:123456789abcdefghi: the scheme did, the name of a DID method, here example, and an identifier that is specific to the method (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022). In a DID URL, which is such an identifier followed by further parts written in the generic syntax, a path, a query and a fragment may follow, as RFC 3986 allows: for instance did:example:123456/path or did:example:123456?versionId=1 (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

Splitting the example at the colons gives three parts, which the chapter's checks print: did, example and the method-specific identifier. The scheme says which specification governs the rest of the string, the method says how to find the document that belongs to it, and the last part is what the method uses to look it up. Software that knows nothing about the method can still parse the string into these pieces because of the generic syntax (Berners-Lee et al., 2005).

A URI names a resource; it does not say that the resource exists or that anybody controls it. Two different strings may name the same resource, and a name that looks like a web address need not lead to a page. For a decentralized identifier the question of who controls the name is answered by the method and by the keys in the document, as the next concept explains.

nodes.definition: A URI is a compact sequence of characters that identifies an abstract or physical resource; the identifiers of the DID standard are URIs of the form did, a colon, a method name, a colon and a method-specific identifier.

nodes.label: Decentralized identifier (DID)
nodes.body: A decentralized identifier, abbreviated DID, is a new type of identifier defined by a recommendation of the World Wide Web Consortium that enables verifiable, decentralised digital identity. A DID refers to any subject, such as a person, an organisation or a thing, as determined by the controller of the DID. DIDs are URIs that associate a DID subject with a DID document, which allows trustable interactions with that subject (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

paras.text: A decentralized identifier, abbreviated DID, is a new type of identifier defined by a recommendation of the World Wide Web Consortium that enables verifiable, decentralised digital identity. A DID refers to any subject, such as a person, an organisation or a thing, as determined by the controller of the DID. DIDs are URIs that associate a DID subject with a DID document, which allows trustable interactions with that subject (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

The standard was designed so that its identifiers may be decoupled from centralised registries, identity providers and certificate authorities. While other parties might help in the discovery of information about a DID, the design enables the controller of a DID to prove control over it without requiring permission from any other party (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022). This is the property that a Bitcoin key pair also has, and it is why the course treats the two together.

A DID document contains information associated with a DID. Each document can express cryptographic material, verification methods or services, which provide a set of mechanisms by which a DID controller can prove control of the DID (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022). A verification method is typically a public key that can authenticate or authorise interactions, and a cryptographic public key can be used with a digital signature to verify that the signer could use the associated private key (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

The specification defines the syntax of a DID, a data model, the core properties, serialised representations and operations, and the process of resolving a DID to the document that it represents; the steps of resolution are defined by the specification of each DID method (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022). The chapter's checks read the abstract and the terminology of the saved specification and confirm the sentences quoted here. A Bitcoin key pair maps to the idea in a simple way: the public key is the verification method, and a signature is the proof of control.

A DID is not a Bitcoin address, and a Bitcoin address is not a DID; they only share the design idea. A DID is meaningful only together with a DID method that says how documents are created, resolved, updated and deactivated, and the method may use a blockchain or may not. The specification speaks of a controller who can prove control, and, as for any key-based scheme, a controller who loses the key loses the ability to prove it.

nodes.example: a DID and its DID document
nodes.definition: A decentralized identifier is a URI that associates a subject with a DID document that can carry verification methods such as public keys, so its controller can prove control without permission from another party.
