findings: Background

Chapter 4 follows a payment's receiver from the private key, a random number, to the public key by elliptic curve multiplication, to the ways a public key becomes something a payer can type: the original pay to public key, the P2PKH commitment in base58check, compressed keys, P2SH, and the bech32 and bech32m segwit addresses, with private key formats, vanity addresses and paper wallets at the end.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's worked example reproduces in full, and from three independent directions: for the private key 1E99...AEDD a Python toolkit written for this chapter gives the book's public key coordinates, its compressed and uncompressed forms, both P2PKH addresses and both WIF strings; Bitcoin Core 31.1 gives the same two addresses from the public keys and from the WIF strings through descriptors and validates every address the chapter prints; and the book's own bech32 reference library gives its four segwit addresses, as does the toolkit, which also passes all 8 valid and 15 invalid BIP350 segwit vectors.
Comparative analysis

One statement in the chapter does not match its primary source: the book says secp256k1 was established by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, but the curve is defined in SEC 2 of the Standards for Efficient Cryptography, published by Certicom Research, and that document's Table 2 marks secp256k1 as not among the NIST-recommended curves while secp256r1 is.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's vanity-address table is exact in its frequencies from one to ten characters and gives 23 quintillion for eleven where 58 to the eleventh is 25 quintillion; its search times follow the rule average time equals half the frequency over 100,000 keys a second for patterns up to seven characters and are about a third shorter than that rule gives from eight characters on: 13 to 18 years against 20, 800 years against 1,180, 46,000 against 68,000 and 2.5 million against 4.0 million.
Comparative analysis

The bech32 error guarantees the chapter cites hold on the book's own P2WPKH address: of the 1,209 substitutions of one character of its 39-character data part and the 712,101 substitutions of two characters, which the claims of this version enumerate exhaustively, not one still carries a valid checksum, and neither does any of the 100,000 random substitutions of three or four characters that they draw from a fixed seed, and the six length-extension strings the chapter prints carry a valid bech32 checksum and no valid bech32m checksum.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's collision-attack figures need updating to the network as it is: the book puts all miners at about 2 to the 80 hashes an hour in early 2023 and 2 to the 128 hashes at about 32 billion years, while a third party's estimate of the hash rate now is about 2.8 times that hourly figure and puts 2 to the 128 hashes at about 11 billion years.
Comparative analysis

Two statements of the interrupted earlier draft of this version did not survive execution and were corrected: the draft said that the SHA-256 digests of the one-bit-apart inputs 'a' and the character before it differ in 126 of their 256 bits, where the interpreter gives 139; and it described the book's six length-extension strings as having 14, 18, 20, 22, 24 and 26 characters formed by adding two letters q at a time, where the book's strings have 15, 18, 20, 22, 23 and 25 characters, formed by inserting three, five, seven, eight and ten letters q before the final p. Both figures are now computed by claims that the chapter builder executes.
Conclusion

For the course theme, a key pair is an identifier whose holder can prove control without asking anyone, the property W3C's Decentralized Identifiers are designed around: a DID is a URI that associates a subject with a DID document that can carry cryptographic material such as verification methods, and its controller can prove control without permission from any other party.
Contemporary developments

The bech32 family the chapter presents is now deployed: the BIPs repository gives BIP173 and BIP350 the status Deployed, Bitcoin Core 31.1 hands out bech32 P2WPKH addresses by default, bech32m taproot addresses on request, and validates the chapter's typo and length-extension examples as the book describes, locating the two typing errors at positions 25 and 40 and refusing all six strings that carry only a bech32 checksum after a version 1 witness.
Contemporary developments

The wallet the owner's notes drive with getnewaddress and dumpprivkey has changed: the 31.1 release still creates addresses but no longer knows dumpprivkey or importprivkey, which the 30.0 release notes list among the removed legacy wallet RPCs, and its default address is a bech32 P2WPKH address rather than the 1J7... address of the notes; a single WIF key can still be turned into an address through a descriptor such as pkh(WIF).
Course notes

The owner's course material for this chapter (2021, written on the 2nd edition), whose text was read for this version, adds topics the 3rd edition's chapter no longer carries or treats differently, each checked: generating a private key with the operating system's random source, for which Python's documentation recommends the secrets module over the random module; the passphrase-protected key of BIP38, which the BIPs repository still marks Deployed but with the comment summary Unanimously Discourage for implementation; the Bitcoin Core commands getnewaddress and dumpprivkey (see the finding on the wallet); and vanity pools and paper wallets, which the 3rd edition keeps but calls obsolete or almost gone.
Known limit

Known limit of the chapter page. The quality gate that governs this chapter's ontology is a SHACL shape file, sen0401_ch04_domain_shacl_v1_1_1.ttl, which states 7 node shapes: that every individual carries a label, that anything defined cites its source, and that a worked example carries exactly one input and one output. The chapter builder applies those shapes to the TBox and the ABox before it writes them, and the build fails if they are violated, so the gate does run; what it does not do is reach the student. The interactive page embeds the chapter's TBox, ABox, document and this research record as Turtle, and the shape file is not among them, so a reader who opens the page can read the ontology it teaches from but cannot read, query or re-run the gate that admitted it, and the page's own list of the triples in each corpus file never mentions the shapes. The limit is recorded here rather than repaired here because the list of files the page embeds is set by the page build chain, which this chapter does not own; repairing it means adding the shape file to that chain's corpus list, after which this finding should be revised to say that the gate is shipped.
Methodology

Terms used without definition: an audit of the vocabulary of every explanation against the concepts of this chapter and of chapters 1 to 3 found terms that the text used without a concept of its own, and version 1.1.0 adds 46 concepts, those terms together with the subject groups that hold them: DigitalSignature, Entropy, FiniteField, EllipticCurve, PointAddition, CurveStandard, GeneratorPoint, DiscreteLogarithm, CryptoLibrary, Hashing, HashFunction, Sha256, Ripemd160, Hash160, Representation, BitsAndBytes, NumberBase, QrCode, CompressedPrivateKey, Checksum, NetworkSelector, Scripts, OutputScript, InputScript, StackExecution, IpAddressPayment, P2pk, RedeemScript, MultisigScript, PreimageAttack, SecondPreimageAttack, CollisionAttack, SegwitUpgrade, NestedSegwit, WitnessVersion, HumanReadablePart, BchCode, LengthExtension, P2wpkh, P2wsh, P2tr, DeterministicWallet, AddressReuse, HardwareSigningDevice, IndependentCheck, Uri. The audit compared a list of cryptographic, Bitcoin and computing terms with the whole text and with the concept labels of this and the earlier chapters, and the terms that remained after the first pass (the coinbase transaction, the cofactor of a curve, the network's rate of hashing and the DID URL) were either given a definition where they are first used or replaced by plain wording, so that no term of the list is now used unexplained.
Methodology

Every sentence that this version takes from a source is re-read from a saved copy of that source by a claim, and every number, hash, address, script, encoding and size it prints is computed: the corpus of version 1.1.0 carries 467 executed claims, among them 64 worked examples whose output the page recomputes in the reader's browser, 15 claims that something fails and 12 error conditions attached to the concept that explains them. The chapter builder refuses to write the ontology unless all of them hold.

stories.title: The 1976 paper that split the key in two
stories.who: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, the Stanford researchers who wrote the paper and received the Turing Award for it
stories.where: IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, volume IT-22, number 6
stories.story: Two Stanford researchers, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, sent a paper called 'New Directions in Cryptography' to the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, which stamped the manuscript received on 3 June 1976 and printed it in its November issue. It opens with a sentence that aged well: we stand today on the brink of a revolution in cryptography. Their idea, a key split into a public half and a private half tied by a one-way computation, is the exact machinery this chapter runs: multiply a point, publish the result, keep the multiplier. Forty years after the paper the ACM gave them its Turing Award for it.
stories.lesson: Every address in this chapter stands on one 1976 idea

stories.title: Why 58? Satoshi left the reasons in the file
stories.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, named by the file's own copyright line
stories.where: src/base58.h in the bitcoin/bitcoin source tree
stories.story: Open src/base58.h in the source tree this course pins and the first thing after the copyright lines - 'Copyright (c) 2009-2010 Satoshi Nakamoto' - is a design memo. Why base-58 and not base-64? Because 0, O, I and l look alike in some fonts; because punctuation breaks selection and line-wrapping; because an all-alphanumeric string survives e-mail and double-clicks whole. The same four reasons stand in the original source of 2009, which Satoshi announced as version 0.1 on 8 January 2009. Four human reasons, zero mathematics - the alphabet of every legacy address is a usability decision, documented by its author in the code itself.
stories.lesson: Address formats are human-factors engineering, documented in the source
stories.source: src/base58.h at the corpus-pinned commit 05bc2f53 of bitcoin/bitcoin: the copyright line naming Satoshi Nakamoto (2009-2010) and the 'Why base-58 instead of standard base-64' comment, quoted verbatim on the slide (MIT); the same comment, with 'account number' for 'data', in src/base58.h of the 0.1.x source of 2009 (github.com/trottier/original-bitcoin, readme.txt: BitCoin v0.1.3 ALPHA). The anchor date is the announcement of version 0.1 (metzdowd.com, 2009-01-08); the day the memo was written is not recorded. stories.title: The address that eats coins
stories.who: Blockstream Explorer, whose address page and API recorded the deposits of thousands of anonymous senders
stories.where: the Bitcoin main chain, at address 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE
stories.story: Spell a message inside an address, append a valid checksum, and you get 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE - a perfectly valid address whose matching key nobody has, because it was chosen as text, not derived from a key. People send coins to it anyway: at this build it held 13.41747849 BTC across 5,832 deposits, and not one satoshi has ever left. The checksum protects you from mistyping an address; nothing protects coins sent to an address that commits to no key.
stories.lesson: An address is a commitment to a key - not proof one exists

The source is Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 22(6), November 1976; ACM A.M.
lecture.takeaway: Public and private halves - one 1976 idea under every address

lecture.title: A private key is just a number
lecture.say: A private key is simply a number, picked at random. Control over the private key is the root of user control over all funds associated with the corresponding public key: the key is used to create the signatures that spend bitcoins by proving control of the funds used in a transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: why is a password a bad private key even if it is long? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Private key and Entropy.
lecture.takeaway: Any 256-bit number - the hard part is choosing it unpredictably

lecture.title: The curve everyone agreed on
lecture.say: The name secp256k1 identifies the specific elliptic curve and the set of constants that Bitcoin uses. The curve is y squared = x cubed + 7 over a finite field of prime order p, with p = 2 to the 256 minus 2 to the 32 minus 2 to the 9 minus 2 to the 8 minus 2 to the 7 minus 2 to the 6 minus 2 to the 4 minus 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Secp256k1 and Generator point.
lecture.takeaway: secp256k1: two primes, one base point, shared by all

lecture.title: Double-and-add: the one-way street
lecture.say: Elliptic curve multiplication takes a point P and a whole number k and produces kP, which is defined as P + P + P + ... + P with k terms. A question to think about is this: where exactly does 'easy forward, hard backward' live in these 13 lines? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Point multiplication and Discrete logarithm.
lecture.takeaway: 256 doublings forward - and no known road back

lecture.title: Prove the key without showing it
lecture.say: A digital signature is a number that a signer computes from a message and from a private key. Anyone who has the message, the signature and the matching public key can verify the signature, that is, can check that it was produced by the holder of the private key and that the message has not been altered since. A question to think about is this: what would 'showing the key' even mean here? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Digital signature and Key control proof.
lecture.takeaway: Chapter 1's house key, kept honest: sign, never reveal

lecture.title: Formats
lecture.say: This branch is about writing the same information down in different ways. A private key, a public key and a hash commitment are all numbers, and a number can be shown in binary, in hexadecimal, in a compact alphabet with a built-in checksum, or in a two-dimensional barcode. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Format.
lecture.takeaway: The same numbers, dressed to travel

lecture.title: Why 58? Satoshi left the reasons in the file
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 2009-2010. Open src/base58.h in the source tree this course pins and the first thing after the copyright lines - 'Copyright (c) 2009-2010 Satoshi Nakamoto' - is a design memo. Why base-58 and not base-64?
lecture.takeaway: The address alphabet is usability engineering, documented

lecture.title: From key to WIF and back
lecture.say: The wallet import format, abbreviated WIF, is the text form in which a private key is exported from one wallet and imported into another. It is the base58check encoding of the version byte 0x80 followed by the 32-byte private key, and, for keys that produce compressed public keys, an extra byte 01 at the end (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Think about this case: decode a WIF by eye: which characters can never appear? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Wallet import format and Compressed private key.
lecture.takeaway: WIF is the same number, dressed for transport

lecture.title: The checksum that catches your typo
lecture.say: A checksum is a short value derived from a piece of data and attached to it. Anyone who has the data and the attached value can recompute the check and see whether they still agree; if the data was altered, they will with overwhelming probability disagree. A question to think about is this: what does the checksum NOT protect you from? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Checksum and Base58Check.
lecture.takeaway: Four bytes stop a mistyped address from costing coins

lecture.title: Addresses
lecture.say: This branch turns the keys of the first branch into something one person can hand to another. An address is a short string that a receiver gives to a payer so that the payer's wallet can build a transaction output that only the receiver can spend. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Address.
lecture.takeaway: Commitments you can read out loud

lecture.title: From public key to address, exactly
lecture.say: A pay to public key hash address, abbreviated P2PKH, is the legacy address in which the output script commits to the HASH160 of the receiver's public key. The output script is OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <commitment> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG and the spender's input script is the signature followed by the public key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: why hash the key at all? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in P2pkh address and Hash160.
lecture.takeaway: Two hashes and an alphabet - the pipeline, executed

lecture.title: The address that eats coins
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated since 2011; balance fetched 2026-10-06. Spell a message inside an address, append a valid checksum, and you get 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE - a perfectly valid address whose matching key nobody has, because it was chosen as text, not derived from a key. People send coins to it anyway: at this build it held 13.41747849 BTC across 5,832 deposits, and not one satoshi has ever left.
lecture.takeaway: An address commits to a key - it cannot conjure one

lecture.title: SegWit and bech32: the second alphabet
lecture.say: Segregated witness, or segwit, is an upgrade that moves signatures and scripts into a separate structure called the witness, committed to blocks apart from the tree of transactions (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The witness holds the data needed to check that a transaction is valid, but not the data that decides what the transaction does. Bech32 gives these outputs an alphabet without look-alike characters, so reading an address aloud no longer invites the old mistakes. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Segwit upgrade and Bech32Address.
lecture.takeaway: New addresses move the witness and drop the look-alikes

lecture.title: Error detection, measured
lecture.say: Error detection is the property of a format that lets software notice that a string has been altered by an accident, such as a mistyped character. A question to think about is this: why does 'provably catches' beat 'has never missed so far'? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Error detection and Bch code.
lecture.takeaway: bech32m catches what base58 provably misses

lecture.title: Taproot, and what wallets do today
lecture.say: Pay to taproot, abbreviated P2TR, is the output kind of segwit version 1. For a P2TR output the witness program is a point on the secp256k1 curve. A question to think about is this: which prefix will your first wallet hand you? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in P2tr and Default address type.
lecture.takeaway: A real wallet's defaults, read from the node

lecture.title: Practice
lecture.say: This branch asks what a user or a developer should do with the material of the earlier branches today. The chapter ends with advanced keys and addresses, vanity addresses and paper wallets, and it surrounds them with remarks about how practice has changed since the first Bitcoin software. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Practice.
lecture.takeaway: Habits that keep keys safe

lecture.title: Habits the chapter prescribes
lecture.say: Address reuse is the practice of receiving more than one payment to the same address. Because all the transactions are public, every payment to an address is visible together with every other payment to it. Think about this case: if one seed makes every address, what single thing must you back up? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Address reuse and Deterministic wallet.
lecture.takeaway: Fresh address every time; the wallet derives, you back up once

lecture.title: The chapter in five lines
lecture.say: Five lines, one per part; the agenda names the slides that prove each. A question to think about is this: which line would you defend first, and with which slide? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in every section.
lecture.takeaway: If a line feels unproven, its part's slides carry the receipt

lecture.title: Where to go from here
lecture.say: Everything here is free. Open the eater address tonight and watch nothing move, because that standstill is this chapter's whole lesson about commitments. Ask yourself who could explain to a parent why bc1p addresses beat old 1-addresses for reading aloud. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Practice.
